Fortunately, though, they usually prefer to hunt goats, sheep, or wild horses. Red Eagles are known for the deep red hue that accents the tips of their gold-colored plumage. They have scarlet beaks.

aspect.en: A hideous crossbreed of Man and orc, first made by the corrupt wizard Saruman — small in number but capable and deadly, and (with Dunlending blood) able to pass among Men as spies and agents. Toward travellers: cunning and malevolent infiltrators who may hide in plain sight before they strike.

lore.en: Half-orcs are a hideous creation, born of Man and Orc. They are often confused with Uruk-hai, but are a distinct race, small in number but capable and deadly. Their origin is also unclear, although it appears that they were first used by the tainted Wizard Saruman. He still employs them as agents, spies, lieutenants, and special guards. They are particularly effective in Eriador, for Saruman's Half-orcs have Dunlending blood in them and are capable of blending into their societies. Half-orcs are akin to Uruk-hai, but look more like dark Men. They speak Westron quite well (Rank 5), and most know both Orkish (Rank 3) and a little Black Speech (Rank 2). Half-orcs have no restrictions on professions, and get three background points.

aspect.en: A mounted troop of the horse-folk ranging the grass-plains in war or on patrol — swift, disciplined and deadly with spear and bow from the saddle, covering ground no footman can match. Toward travellers: formidable riders; no threat to honest folk, but they will ride down and question strangers on their lands.

lore.en: A mounted troop of the Éothraim horse-folk — riders ranging the grass-plains in war or on patrol, swift and disciplined, deadly with spear and bow from the saddle. Whether a small scouting party or a full éored, they cover ground no footman can match.

aspect.en: The Drúedain — an ancient, diminutive forest-people unmatched in wood-craft and woodland warfare, thought ugly and long persecuted by Men and Elves, surviving hidden in the deep woods. Toward travellers: deeply wary and secretive after ages of hunting; no aggressors, but they watch unseen and trust few — yet stalwart friends to those who earn it.

lore.en: Of all Men, none surpass the Woses in the arts of wood-lore and wood-craft. This very ancient and diminutive race has long been tied to the forests and has remained the greatest lot of woodland warriors ever produced by the Second-born. Their skills have in fact guarded their narrow survival, for they are considered ugly by Men and Elves alike and have been hunted and persecuted since the days of the First Age. The Woses have many names. What they call themselves is not altogether clear, although the name Drûgs is taken from their own tongue. Drúedain (sing. Drúadan) is the label given them by the Elves, while Men call them by various labels: Rógin (sing. "Róg"), Púkelmen, Wild Men, or Woses, the latter a Westron term. Orcs fear the Woses, and have named them Oghor-hai. Physical Character: Woses generally have a broad, stumpy profile marked by wide faces, flat features, and deep-set eyes. Short, thick legs, heavy lower bodies, and pronounced brows help give them an eerie character. Ruddy skin, black hair, and black eyes. 4 to 5 feet. Lifespan: 30-50 years. The wide noses of the Woses are the most sensitive found in Man. Even in an open field, they can smell an Orc before another Man can see him. +25 bonus to Tracking maneuvers; +15 bonus for Foraging. They have the ability to sit for days on end without movement. Woses are blessed with superb night-vision. Even in the dark forest of the night they can see 1000 feet as if it were daylight.

aspect.en: The crowded folk of the fen-ringed river-city of Tharbad — merchants, craftsmen, guildsmen, smugglers and refugees — in a town whose rule has slipped from kings to guilds as flood, war and plague wore it down. Toward travellers: a mixed, bustling, sometimes lawless river-city people; opportunity and risk both, depending whom you meet.

lore.en: Merchants, craftsmen, guildsmen, smugglers and refugees crowd the fen‑ringed city of Tharbad, whose power shifts from Cardolan's kings to Gondor's Canotar and then to powerful guilds as war, flood and plague erode royal authority.[file:31]

aspect.en: A compact, strongly-built bear common in the North — a nocturnal omnivore that gorges before hibernating, with a superb nose but weak eyes and ears; solitary, the female travelling with her cubs. Toward travellers: avoids people, but dangerous if surprised, cornered, or met with cubs.

lore.en: Strongly built but compact bear (Q. "Meglivorn"), common throughout northern Endor. Nocturnal omnivores that gorge before winter hibernation; superb sense of smell but weak hearing/eyesight. Solitary, the female travelling with 1-4 cubs. Eriadoran Northmen, the Lossoth and the Beijabar/Beornings hold near-cultic bear traditions.

aspect.en: Domesticated dogs of Men and Hobbits — here usually the fierce wolfhound, from small farm dogs to great hunting beasts once bred to bring down wolves. Found wherever folk dwell, sometimes gone wild in empty lands. Toward travellers: loyal guardians to their masters, but a wild or guard pack will challenge and harry an intruder.

lore.en: In Middle-earth the term Hound (Q. Huo, pl. Huron) almost always means the fierce Wolfhound, ranging from the diminutive dogs of Hobbit farmers near the Shire to the great noble beasts the Men of old used to hunt Wargs and the werewolves of Morgoth. Found wherever Men or Hobbits dwell, they sometimes run wild in deserted lands. The most famous was Huan of Valinor, one of the immortal hounds of Orome, who followed Celegorm into exile, aided Luthien and Beren, and both slew and was slain by Carcharoth.

aspect.en: A war-band of orcs on the march or raid — dozens of fighters with captains, sometimes mounted or trailing baggage — bound for plunder, slaughter or muster. Toward travellers: a serious threat to any small company; far too strong to fight, best avoided or outrun.

lore.en: A war-band of Orcs on the march or raid — dozens of fighters with their captains, sometimes mounted or trailing a baggage-train. Bound for plunder, slaughter or muster, such a band is a serious threat to any small company that crosses its path.

aspect.en: An enclosed yard, garden or homestead-close — a walled plot of orchard, herb-beds or pasture about a dwelling, a small island of order and plenty. Toward travellers: a likely place to beg food or shelter, and a sign of settled, tended land.

lore.en: An enclosed yard, garden or homestead-close — a walled plot of orchard, herb-beds or pasture about a dwelling. A small island of order and plenty, and a place a traveller might beg food or shelter.

aspect.en: Northmen of the Great River valleys; some of their young warriors take service with the Witch-king's hosts, seeking wealth and glory. Toward travellers: ordinary river-vale folk, though some of their fighting men ride with the Enemy — loyalties to weigh with care.

lore.en: Northmen of the Great River valleys; some young men, especially those with strong warrior values, join the Witch-king's forces seeking wealth and opportunity.

aspect.en: The "Snowmen" of the far north — a sparse, nomadic, cold-hardened folk, stocky and tough, who move with the migrations of big game and rarely deal with other Men. Toward travellers: reclusive and shy of outsiders but not hostile; a rare source of aid and lore in the deadly cold.

lore.en: The Lossoth live in the Far North of western Middle-earth and are often called "Snowmen" or "Forodwaith" (the latter is also a name for their land). They are a sparsely settled, nomadic folk who move with the seasonal migrations of big game and rarely interact with other Men. Physical Character: Stocky and hard, with pronounced muscles. They have wide features and large, pudgy hands and feet. Men average 175 pounds, women 140 pounds. Fair, with reddish highlights. They have pale blue eyes and fair hair. They are extremely rugged and can travel great distances with little or no rest. Short; men average 5'5", women 5'3". Lifespan: Medium, about 75-90 years. +20 bonus versus cold/ice attacks. -20 bonus versus heat/fire attacks. They have an acute sense of smell and perception. They can pick up a Man's scent a mile downwind and 100 feet upwind (1000 feet otherwise). +10 bonus to Perception. The Lossoth are poor, nomadic hunters and gatherers. They use stonework, bone, and limited amounts of wood and metal (mostly copper). Some herd reindeer and all make use of hunting dogs. They hate Wargs, Dragons, Giants, and Trolls above all things.

aspect.en: The "great orcs" — a larger, stronger, more intelligent orc-race bred by the Dark Lord, able to act on their own and endure daylight, serving as elite soldiers and captains. Toward travellers: disciplined, fearless and deadly warriors, among the worst foes on any road — and they do not flee the sun.

lore.en: Following Sauron's resurrection in T.A. 1000 he began breeding a new race of Orcs, one capable of independent and intelligent action. After centuries of work, he produced the first Greater Orcs, and he called them the Uruk-hai (BS "Orc-race") because they were more suited to the formation of societies. Initially, the Uruk-hai remained close to Sauron and served as lieutenants and elite guards, but gradually their numbers grew and their strain strengthened. Their existence remained guarded until Sauron was willing to show his hand. Nonetheless, in T.A. 2475 they were unleashed in full scale battle formations. They are the Dark Lord's finest goblin troops. The Uruk-hai differ from normal or Lesser Orcs in many ways: (1) they stand 5-6 feet tall; (2) they have a more "human" appearance, despite cat-like eyes, fang-teeth, and black/grey hides; (3) they have longer, stronger, and straighter legs; (4) they are intelligent and cunning; and (5) despite their preference for darkness, they operate freely in daylight. They speak Black Speech (Rank 5), Orkish (Rank 4), and good Westron (Rank 4).

aspect.en: Swift, colourful crocodiles (black with green stripes) of warm wetlands — usually idle and inoffensive if left alone, but deadly when surprised or hungry, seizing prey at the water's edge, drowning it and tearing it apart. Toward travellers: a hidden killer along warm marsh-banks; safe at a distance, lethal up close.

lore.en: Swift but usually inactive, the Marsh, or "Fish-eating," Crocodiles are common in the wetter, warmer parts of Endor. They are inoffensive when let alone, but can be quite deadly when surprised (or hungry). Black, with green stripes and light blue undersides, they are colorful carnivores. Their diet consists of large mammals and birds who enter or come to the edge of the water. After grabbing its prey in its long, powerful snout, the Marsh Crocodile drowns the victim and then tears the flaccid body apart with twisting bites. It spends its nights in the water and basks on shore during the day, feeding on average once every two days, and swallows rocks for ballast.

aspect.en: Dwarves working the coal and iron mines on the eastern slopes of the southern Blue Mountains. Toward travellers: industrious, close-mouthed miners; reserved with strangers but no threat to honest folk.

lore.en: Dwarves operating coal and iron mines on the eastern slopes of the southern Blue Mountains.

aspect.en: Large northern deer of forest and marsh, the bulls carrying broad spreading antlers. Usually placid, but powerful and aggressive in the autumn rut, when a bull can match a wolf or gore a careless hunter. Toward travellers: leaves people alone, but rutting bulls deserve a wide berth.

lore.en: Large deer of the northern forests and marshes, the bulls bearing broad spreading antlers. Powerful and aggressive in the rut, an elk (or moose) can be a match for a wolf or a careless hunter.

aspect.en: A dense swarm of biting or stinging insects — flies, midges, gnats or worse — thick enough to torment man and beast, foul wounds and drive cattle mad; the bane of marsh and still summer air. Toward travellers: a maddening, sapping torment that can spoil a march or a camp, especially near stagnant water.

lore.en: A dense swarm of biting or stinging insects — flies, midges, gnats or worse — thick enough to torment beast and man, foul wounds and drive cattle to madness. The bane of marsh and still summer air.

aspect.en: A huge serpent of southern marshes and rivers, long enough to coil and crush a man or a large beast — patient and hidden, striking from the water's edge and dragging prey under. Toward travellers: a lethal ambush at warm waterside; it crushes and drowns whatever it seizes.

lore.en: A huge serpent of the southern marshes and rivers, long enough to coil and crush a man or a large beast. Patient and hidden, it strikes from the water's edge and drags its prey under.

aspect.en: A black-and-purple eagle of the eastern Eriador hills that hunts silently and low, skimming ridges to ambush small prey like gophers and rock-conies. Toward travellers: no real threat to people, though its sudden low rush over a hilltop can badly startle the unwary.

lore.en: The Vereut Eagle inhabits the hills of eastern Eriador. It is black over most of its body and wings, but its hue reaches a dark purple near the face and wing tips. The Eagle beak and eyes stand in stark contrast, for they both are a bright yellow color. When hunting, they fly silently, low to the ground, enabling them to skirt the tops of hills and ridges to surprise their favorite prey: Gophers and Rock Hydrax. This method of hunting is startling to those who are unacquainted with the beasts, and many an Eriadoran has suddenly found himself in a brief, bewildering combat at the crest of a hill. Several Dunlanders wear scars on their faces attesting that these chance meetings can be dangerous.

aspect.en: Social wasp-relatives that nest in cracks and fissures of cliffs, sometimes well toward cave-mouths. Not aggressive unless a nest is disturbed, when the swarm attacks en masse with painful, venomous stings. Toward travellers: a hazard only if one blunders into a nest among the rocks.

lore.en: Relatives of the common Mud Dauber Wasp, Cliff Hornets are social insects who build their nest in cracks, crevices, and fissures in the sides of cliffs. Although they will not build nests deep underground, their homes can sometimes be found as much as several hundred feet from a cave entrance if a good nesting site can be found there. These insects are not normally dangerous unless one is an intruder who has blundered into the midst of a nest. Then the outraged Hornets will attack en masse with their sharp, barbless stingers, injecting the victim with a venom that will, at minimum, cause pain and swelling. In addition, many people are allergic to Cliff Hornet venom and may die from its effects. Note: Treat Hornet venom as a first level poison. A normal, nonallergic reaction is -25 to all actions for 1-30 hours. There is a 35% chance (01-35) of allergic reaction, a percentage that may be modified by the victim's Constitution. In the case of an allergic reaction, an incapacitating fever and respiratory distress will afflict the victim for 1-4 days, and five or more stings may cause death in 1 to 10 hours.

aspect.en: Foul or deadly vapours — marsh-gas, volcanic fumes or the airs of some tainted place — that sicken, stupefy or kill, often unseen and pooling in hollows, caves and stagnant low ground. Toward travellers: an invisible killer; suspect bad air in caves and hollows, and do not linger where the ground stinks.

lore.en: Foul or deadly vapours — marsh-gas, volcanic fumes or the airs of some tainted place — that sicken, stupefy or kill those who breathe them. Often unseen, they pool in hollows, caves and stagnant low ground.

aspect.en: Luring marsh-spirits that appear as a wholesome, alluring vision above the water — each victim sees whatever would draw them in (a fair maid, a lost child, a fat purse) — to lead them to drown in the bog. Toward travellers: a deadly deception of swamp and marsh by night; the beckoning light is a trap.

lore.en: Corpse Lanterns, being both stronger and more i n t e l l i g e n t than Corpse Candles, weave a stronger and more alluring web, appearing whole and wholesome above the waters of the marsh or swamp, and seeming to the victim to be something that would attract his attention. The visions vary according to the victim, and several unfortunates gazing upon the same Corpse Lantern may see different things: the lusty warrior may see a buxom wench with a lantern, searching for something; the compassionate Healer a lost child with a lamp; the suspicious thief a fat merchant with a purse that could use lightening, engaged in burying more treasure in the safe embrace of the marsh. Thus the Corpse Lantern entices its victims to a death by drowning, enabling the undead remnant to drain 5 Co points per round in the interim.

aspect.en: Lesser Maiar of Morgoth's allegiance whose shapes and powers vary without limit, many bound up with raw forces like fire, as Balrogs are. Toward travellers: terribly dangerous; they may sometimes be bargained with, but such bargains rarely end well for the one who makes them.

lore.en: Lesser Maiar allied with Morgoth whose forms and abilities vary infinitely. They can sometimes be persuaded to aid Men or Elves, even in good deeds, but unless the petitioner is carefully protected and binds them with strong constraints little good comes of such bargains; like Balrogs, many partake of natural forces such as fire.

aspect.en: A dog-sized, otter-like creature of the southern woods — short-legged, irrepressibly friendly and playful as a puppy, infamous for cheerfully tearing open foragers' packs; its sheer innocence is what keeps it from being killed. Toward travellers: utterly harmless and endearing, a mischievous pest rather than a danger.

lore.en: In Apysaic, Stetan means "mischievous." It applies perfectly to this otter-like creature. The beast's body is as large as a big dog, and it is as friendly and playful as the most lively of puppies. It has very short legs, though, so no one would mistake it for a hound. The Stetan's name was earned from the Haradrim who journeyed into the wood, worked a long day gathering herbs, then saw their sacks and parcels playfully torn apart just before they returned home. Only their overpowering air of pure innocence keeps Stetanavi from being killed on sight by most men who glean their living from the wood. As it is, they are usually viewed as a sign of long-term good luck even if they are a short-term nuisance. There have been attempts to tame the friendly beasts, but Stetanavi taken into captivity invariably die shortly thereafter, an occurrence usually blamed on loneliness for their own kind. It is possible to overcome this through the use of a Familiar spell, though having such a puckish creature as a familiar would certainly have its drawbacks.

aspect.en: A leopard-like cat of the Far Harad woodlands, smaller than a true leopard and splotched brown for perfect jungle camouflage — prowling the undergrowth and low branches for mostly small, swift prey but able to bring down larger, and able to take a man by surprise. Toward travellers: a stealthy ambush hunter of the jungle that may strike the unwary.

lore.en: Large cat (the Unca) of the hilly woodlands of Far Harad, often the only large mammal in its ecosystem and rather smaller than the Leopard it resembles. Its pelt is splotched in shades of brown for perfect camouflage as it prowls the overgrown jungle floor or hides in low branches; since most local prey is small and quick it spends much time chasing through the brush, though its sturdy build lets it take larger game. It avoids the deadly Petla, hunts the playful Stetan, and will take Men by surprise.

aspect.en: Graves, barrows and tombs of the dead — mounds on the downs, rock-cut sepulchres and old graveyards — shunned after dark, for grave-goods tempt robbers and not every barrow's tenant lies quiet. Toward travellers: a place of dread and temptation; shelter or treasure, but also robbers and the risk of what may not rest.

lore.en: Graves, barrows and tombs of the dead — mounds on the downs, rock-cut sepulchres and old graveyards. Folk shun them after dark, for grave-goods tempt robbers and not every barrow's tenant lies quiet.

aspect.en: Trolls adapted to life underground, dwelling in caves and deep passages and at home in darkness — huge, thick-skinned and savage. Toward travellers: a lethal danger in the dark of caverns and old mines, strong enough to crush an armed party.

lore.en: Trolls that dwell in caves and underground passages, adapted to darkness.

aspect.en: Monstrous web-spinning spiders descended from Ungoliant, lurking in gloomy forests like Mirkwood — cunning enough to speak and to cooperate in trapping prey, which they bind and poison with paralysing, flesh-dissolving venom. The greatest, like Shelob, are horrors in their own right. Toward travellers: deadly ambush predators that snare and devour the unwary in the dark.

lore.en: Web-spinning descendants of Ungoliant; the lesser kind haunt Mirkwood and other gloomy places, speaking Westron and Black Speech and cooperating to trap victims with paralysing then dissolving venom. Greater ones include Shelob, guardian of Cirith Ungol in Mordor, and Enna San Sarab of Dol Guldur.

aspect.en: A patrol of Broadbeam Dwarves warding the roads and mine-approaches of the Blue Mountains — grim and heavily armed, guarding their holds against orcs and trespassers and keeping the old ways open. Toward travellers: stern, watchful guards, correct with honest folk but quick to challenge strangers near their gates.

lore.en: A patrol of Broadbeam Dwarves warding the roads and mine-approaches of the Blue Mountains. Grim and heavily armed, they guard the holds of Nan-i-Naugrim against Orcs and trespassers and keep the old ways open between the Dwarf-towns.

aspect.en: River-folk who ply the Baranduin and other northern rivers, claiming the waters as their own and carrying trade and word between the northern realms. Toward travellers: independent boat-folk, useful for passage and news, but proprietary about their rivers.

lore.en: River-folk who ply the Baranduin and other northern rivers, claiming the waters as their own and serving trade and communication between Arthedain, Lindon and other regions.[file:25]

aspect.en: A body of armed men watching the roads, borders and marches of a realm — soldiers, militia or a lord's riders — challenging strangers and hunting bandits and raiders. Toward travellers: their temper depends on whose land it is and how the times sit — lawful aid or stern suspicion.

lore.en: A body of armed men keeping watch over the roads, borders and marches of a realm — soldiers, militia or a lord's riders, large or small, challenging strangers and hunting bandits and raiders. Their temper depends on whose land it is and how the times sit.

aspect.en: Farmers and nomads of the Vale of Harnen, growing sorghum and herding flocks and moving seasonally between Harad and the southern plateaus — a lasting presence even where Gondor claims rule. Toward travellers: southern country folk of contested borderlands, their welcome shifting with loyalties and the season.

lore.en: Haruze farmers and nomads who have occupied the Vale of Harnen, growing sorghum and herding flocks, moving seasonally between Harad/Nurn and the southern Harondor plateau; a persistent cultural presence even when Gondor claims political control.[file:73]

aspect.en: Dull-witted cousins of the evil Crebain — not malicious, just indifferent and endlessly hungry, with a magpie's lust for shiny things; their messy communal nests are often littered with hoarded coins and trinkets. Toward travellers: harmless singly, but they band together fiercely to defend a nest, so plundering their trove is risky.

lore.en: Smaller cousins of the evil Crebain, Gorcrows are not so much evil as indifferent to suffering. Not nearly as bright as their larger cousins, Gorcrows live to eat (although, if asked, they would probably insist that they merely eat to live). They are attracted to shiny things, and Gorcrows have picked up unbelievable numbers of shiny trinkets and small coins. Their untidy, communal nesting sites are often littered with minor yet still significant amounts of wealth. However, since Gorcrows will cooperate in protecting their nest sites, would-be plunderers are well-advised to be very cautious and to wear helmets with small eyeslits: Gorcrows are notoriously fond of eyeballs!

aspect.en: A wary snow-people who roam the northern wastes from spring to autumn, camping rough on rocky slopes for days at a time, reserved with strangers and apter to move on than to deal with rough folk. Toward travellers: shy and cautious, but approached gently they can give detailed knowledge of the land, its hazards and its ways.

lore.en: The Lumënyihmënyt roam the northernmost stretches of the Rammas Forod from early spring through mid-autumn. Their camps, perched on rocky slopes, are crude hunting sites intended to last days or at most weeks. Reserved and wary, they usually break camp and move rather than deal with rough strangers, but if approached carefully they can provide detailed information about local geography, hazards and notable features.

aspect.en: Odd wild goats of the plains south of Mirkwood — near-untamable, sometimes grazing in mixed herds with wild horses, and immune to all natural ingested poisons so they can feed on almost anything. Toward travellers: harmless and intractable, a curiosity of the eastern plains.

lore.en: The Fintónarki, or Wild Goats, are odd beasts found on the plains south of Mirkwood. They have several characteristics that set them apart from the other Goats of Middle-earth. For one thing, they are sometimes found in mixed herds with the Wild Horses of the area, an arrangement found nowhere else. Second, they are almost untamable, although it is reported that Elves may have some success at this task. Third, they are immune to all naturally occuring ingestible poisons and hence can live on almost anything that contains nourishment. Finally, these strange creatures have an unquenchable desire to be scratched on the head, between their long, dangerous horns. It is rumored among various denizens of the Talath Harroch region (particularly those with small, naïve children) that if one should do one of these hoofed hedonists the favor of scratching it in the proper spot, it will become ever loyal to the person who scratches it. This tale has caused numerous injuries to youngsters seeking an unusual pet.

aspect.en: Lightly-armed men ranging ahead of a larger force or watching a stretch of country — outriders, foresters and trackers in someone's service, keeping out of sight and carrying word swiftly back. Toward travellers: watchful and elusive; whether they help or hinder depends on whom they serve.

lore.en: Lightly-armed men ranging ahead of a larger force or watching a stretch of country — outriders, foresters and trackers in someone's service. They keep out of sight, mark the movements of friend and foe, and carry word swiftly back.

aspect.en: Tall, closely-spaced hardwoods with bare lower trunks and umbrella-crowns high overhead, their dense canopies and thick bark making the inner woods of Southern Mirkwood dark and damp. Toward travellers: not dangerous in themselves, but they make the forest gloomy, close and easy to get lost in.

lore.en: Tall, closely spaced hardwoods with branchless lower trunks and umbrella crowns about forty feet up. Their dense canopies and thick bark make Southern Mirkwood's interior dark, damp and resistant to many pests and blights.

aspect.en: Large stinging insects that build papery nests in trees and eaves and defend them ferociously. A disturbed nest can drive off a bear or a horse, and a storm of stings is dangerous even to a grown man. Toward travellers: a real hazard if a nest is struck or camped beside unawares.

lore.en: Large stinging insects of wood and eave that nest in papery combs and defend them fiercely. A disturbed nest can drive off a bear or a horse, and a storm of stings is dangerous even to a grown man.

aspect.en: Rowdy, semi-independent clans of the Gwathló mouthlands, their culture a blend of Dunnish ways and refugee influences — providing both raiders and stubborn defenders. Toward travellers: unruly and unpredictable; some hospitable, some quick to rob, depending on the clan and the day.

lore.en: Rowdy, semi‑independent clans of Saralainn and the Gwathló mouthlands whose culture blends Dunnish traditions and refugee influences, often providing both raiders and hardy defenders in the south.[file:31]

aspect.en: Picked orc warriors — bigger, better-armed and grimly disciplined — set to guard a captain, a fortress gate or some business of the Enemy, far more dangerous than common goblins. Toward travellers: hostile and deadly; they kill or capture intruders without parley.

lore.en: Picked Orc warriors, bigger and better-armed than the common run, set to guard a captain, a fortress gate or some matter of the Enemy's; Sauron's own guards among them are grimly disciplined and far more dangerous than ordinary goblins.

aspect.en: Rats of cellar, midden and ruin, thriving wherever folk leave food and filth — quick-breeding and bold. Toward travellers: spoil stores and carry sickness, and in old tunnels and dungeons can swarm in unsettling numbers.

lore.en: Rats of cellar, midden and ruin, thriving wherever folk leave food and filth. Quick-breeding and bold, they spoil stores, carry sickness, and in old tunnels and dungeons can swarm in alarming numbers.

aspect.en: A scattered folk of huge, immensely strong men akin to the Woodmen — exceedingly hairy and fair-skinned herders, bee-keepers and woodsmen of the Anduin vales, some said to take bear-shape. Toward travellers: independent and hospitable to friends but fierce to foes, keeping the river-lands clear of orcs and wolves.

lore.en: Also called Beijabar or Bajaegahar, this dispersed group of large men has a confused origin. They are a Northmen branch related to the Woodmen, Lake-men, and Dale-men of Rhovanion, although they apparently became distinct in elder times, probably before the Northman migrations out of Eriador. Physical Character: Physically, the Beornings are the largest of the Northmen, and all are strong of build and bone structure. Men are exceedingly hairy; they average 220 pounds. Women average 145 pounds. Their complexions are fair, but unlike most Northmen (who are usually blond), the majority have reddish hair. Beornings need sleep only twice every three days. Men average 6'4", women 5'7". Lifespan: 80-100 years. Wild animals will not attack a Beorning unless actively provoked. They are extremely hairy, and their tendency to wear furs gives them an "animal-like" appearance. Beornings have traditionally lived in small groups or single families on well-tended "manors". Some, like Beorn's line, have favored relative lowlands, while the majority reside in the passes and foothills of the Misty Mountains or Grey Mountains. Beornings hate Orcs, Wargs, Trolls, Giants, and Dragons.

aspect.en: A wild golden bighorn sheep found only in the Downs of Eriador, with long curving pale horns — solitary and intractable, gathering only to mate, and prized for cross-breeding with domestic flocks. Toward travellers: harmless and aloof, a rare handsome sight on the high downs.

lore.en: Goral are a wild, golden bighorn Sheep found exclusively in the Downs of Eriador. They have long, curving, whitish horns. Solitary and intractable, they are unique among Sheep. Goral only gather during mating season, when small groups of males join and then seek out the females. Ranked by the size of their horns, the males instinctively know their place, so there is little fighting during these brief unions. After mating, the females travel as a herd with the young for a couple of months and then scatter. Goral have been very profitably interbred with domestic Sheep, producing excellent varieties of wool-bearing species (Q. "Toa" = "Wool").

aspect.en: The High Men of Gondor's coast, whose power is rooted in Pelargir and the seaward towns — commanders of fleets and rulers of the province, leading the long fight against Corsairs and Haradan raiders. Toward travellers: proud, authoritative lords of the sea-coast, correct with strangers and watchful for enemies from the water.

lore.en: High Men of Gondor, especially the Sea-lords whose power is rooted in Pelargir and the coastal towns; they command fleets, administer the province and lead the struggle against Corsairs and Haradan privateers.[file:30]

aspect.en: A small community of Stoor hobbits living in burrows on marsh-hills, travelling by pole-boat and trading herbs and fish, shielded by treacherous wetlands and their own wariness. Toward travellers: shy, peaceable marsh-hobbits, slow to trust outsiders but no threat.

lore.en: A small Stoor Hobbit community living in burrows on hills rising from a marsh near the Dunstrem, traveling by pole‑boats, trading herbs and fish, and protected by the treacherous wetlands and their own wariness of outsiders.[file:32]

aspect.en: Dunlending-kin highlanders of the Ered Tarthonion, descended from the mountain Daen — rugged village folk under their own chieftains, paying tribute in kind, keeping animist and sometimes dark rites and resisting outside ways. Toward travellers: insular and wary of strangers, clinging to old customs; suspicious, but not always hostile.

lore.en: Dunlending‑related highlanders of the Ered Tarthonion, descendants of the Daen Coentis; rugged village dwellers ruled by their own chieftains, paying tribute in kind, practicing animistic and sometimes dark rites and resisting assimilation.

aspect.en: A medium-sized, tuft-eared wildcat of the northern forests, hunting hares, birds and small deer — solitary, elusive and keeping to dense cover, more often heard than seen. Toward travellers: shy and no threat to people, a fleeting shadow among the trees.

lore.en: A medium-sized, tuft-eared wildcat of the northern forests, hunting hares, birds and small deer. Solitary and elusive, it keeps to dense cover and is more often heard than seen.

aspect.en: Squat, fat little hounds kept only by the Dunlendings, used after a fashion as guards or pack-hunters but poor at both — and as often as not ending in the cooking-pot. Toward travellers: harmless and unimpressive, a sign of a Dunlending camp more than any threat.

lore.en: Squat dogs resembling a large, fat toy hound, kept only by the tribal Dunlendings. Sometimes used as guards or for pack-hunting, at which they are marginally capable; most Dunmen's Dogs end up in the stewpot.

aspect.en: A great slow river of ice riddled with hidden crevasses, unstable ice-towers and meltwater channels — a peril to cross, with bitter cold and blinding glare adding to the danger. Toward travellers: treacherous footing where a hidden crevasse can swallow a careless step; not to be crossed lightly.

lore.en: A great river of ice, slow-moving and riddled with hidden crevasses, unstable séracs and meltwater channels. Crossing one is a peril in itself, and the bitter cold and glare add to the danger.

aspect.en: A wolf-like wild hill-dog of the arid south, mottled tan and grey for camouflage, with a wolf's strength and a jackal's boldness — pack-hunters that run prey to exhaustion, circling and yelping until even tough wild goats fall, turning to carrion when game is scarce. Toward travellers: a persistent, dangerous pack-predator of dry country.

lore.en: Wild hill dog of the arid and semi-arid hills of southern Endor, abundant in Far Harad, Chy, Vaag and Gaathgykarkan and ranging east to Horl. It resembles a wolf but with a larger, squarer snout and a mottled dark-tan coat spotted grey and brown for camouflage. With a wolf's strength and a jackal's pride it is resilient, hunting in packs and turning to carrion when game is scarce; rather than ambush it runs prey to exhaustion, circling and giving off yelping barks until even the region's tough wild goats fall.

aspect.en: Flying cold-drakes of the northern mountains, notably the Grey Mountains, that raid Dwarven halls. Toward travellers: a winged, fireless dragon — vast, cold and rapacious, striking from the peaks.

lore.en: Winged Cold-drakes, like Fire-drakes, descend from the true Cold-drakes; they keep to northern mountain lairs (notably the Grey Mountains) and raid Dwarven settlements.

aspect.en: An organized force of soldiery on the move — a company, column or picked band marching to muster, garrison or war under its captains; disciplined and well-armed. Toward travellers: no foe for a small party and brooking no interference — lawful or hostile by whose banner it bears.

lore.en: An organized force of soldiery on the move — a company, column or picked elite band, marching to muster, garrison or war under its captains. Disciplined and well-armed, it is no foe for a small party and brooks no interference on the road.

aspect.en: A sheer drop or precipice where a single misstep means a fatal fall, barring the way along coasts, gorges and mountain paths. Toward travellers: a real and silent danger — a crumbling edge or sudden gust can send the careless over.

lore.en: A sheer drop or precipice where a single misstep means a fatal fall. Cliffs bar the way along coasts, gorges and mountain paths, and a crumbling edge or sudden gust can send the careless over.

aspect.en: Men who range the northern woods trapping beasts for pelts — solitary, hardy and weather-worn, coming to town only to sell furs and resupply before vanishing back into the trees. Toward travellers: gruff loners and no threat, a possible source of guidance and trade in the deep wilds.

lore.en: Men who range the northern woods and wilds trapping beasts for their pelts — solitary, hardy and weather-worn, coming to town only to sell furs and lay in supplies before vanishing back into the trees.

aspect.en: Small, long-lived descendants of the Edain dwelling in the western marshes, living by hunting, fishing, goat-herding and gardening and governed by yearly councils on a holy island; some driven west by the marshes' corruption. Toward travellers: a reclusive, peaceable fen-folk, keeping to their waters and wary of outsiders.

lore.en: Small, long-lived descendants of the Edain dwelling in Nindalf and western marshes, living by hunting, fishing, goat herding and gardening, worshipping Eru (Iroi) and the Valar as Jevinn and Eremi, and organizing themselves through yearly councils on the holy island of Tel Belarin; some have been driven westward by the Dead Marshes' corruption.[file:37]

aspect.en: A large aquatic snake of central Endor's marshes — the Dead Marshes and Wetwang above all — an excellent swimmer whose mottled grey-brown scales hide it in foul water; easily startled and quick to bite, with long fangs and deep-striking venom. Toward travellers: a real hazard of wading the marshes, biting with little provocation.

lore.en: The Marsh Adder is a large, aquatic serpent common throughout all marshy areas of central Endor. Especially prevalent in the Dead Marshes and Nindalf (the Wetwang), this creature is an excellent swimmer whose mottled gray and brown scales allow it to go all but unnoticed in the foul waters of the marshes. Marsh Adders are easily startled and bite with little provocation, usually seeking out small creatures such as ducklings and frogs but also attacking larger beings if threatened. Its large, curved fangs deliver its poison deeply. The (10th lvl) venom can be lethal: many victims (RR failure of 51+) die in five rounds due to respiratory paralysis, while a less imposing dose (RR failure 01-50) gives flaccid paralysis, leaving the joints limp and the victim without voluntary muscle control for 1-100 hours.

aspect.en: A fortified tower set to watch a road, ford, border or pass — manned in good times, ruinous or ill-held in bad; from its top a long stretch of country is watched. Toward travellers: shelter and lawful aid if friendly-held, a trap or a watching eye if it has fallen — and you are rarely unseen beneath it.

lore.en: A fortified tower set to watch a road, ford, border or pass — manned in good times, ruinous or ill-held in bad. From its top a long stretch of country can be watched, and travellers below are seldom unseen.

aspect.en: Folk of Dyr in the eastern marches near the Sea of Rhûn — traders, herders and rivermen living between the great realms, prizing their wine, horses and hard-won independence. Toward travellers: proud, self-reliant border-folk; fair traders, wary of being ruled.

lore.en: Folk of Dyr in the eastern marches near Dorwinion and the Sea of Rhûn — traders, herders and rivermen living between the great realms, prizing their wine, horses and hard-won independence.

aspect.en: Descendants of Gondorian rebels who fled to Umbar after the Kin-strife — strong-built, mostly fair Dúnedain stock, long warring with the southern peoples and burning to reclaim Gondor. Toward travellers: hostile sea-raiders and enemies of Gondor, pirates who plunder the coasts and take captives.

lore.en: The Corsairs are descendants of the Dúnedain rebels who fled from Gondor in the wake of the Kin-strife of T.A. 1432-47. Most settled in Umbar in T.A. 1447 and began a long struggle for control with the stronger Haradan and Black Númenorean elements. Since that time modest inbreeding with the locals has created a somewhat distinct group, although their Dúnedain roots remain strong. They long to reclaim Gondor as their own. Physical Character: Strong of build; males average 220 pounds, women 145 pounds. Corsairs are generally fair skinned and have grey or bluish eyes and black or dark brown hair. Considerable endurance. They do not get seasick. Men average 6'3", women 5'9". Lifespan: 95-190 years. +25 bonus for Weather-watching or Star-gazing activity. Corsairs favor purple, red, and gold clothing made from silk or fine cotton. They wear tunics and only rarely don leggings. Men wear gold collars, while women are well-adorned with jewelry. Corsair culture reflects the conservative elements found among Gondor's aristocracy, only it is carried to an extreme.

aspect.en: The native pre-Númenórean people of the coasts and plains — shorter and stockier than the Dúnedain — who took up Westron and Númenórean ways while keeping their old songs and lore; they make up most of the common folk of Lebennin and Anfalas. Toward travellers: settled, ordinary country people whose welcome ranges from hospitable to wary.

lore.en: The indigenous pre-Númenórean people of the coastlands and plains, shorter and stockier than the Dúnedain, who adopted Westron and much of Númenórean culture while retaining their oral traditions and ballads; they form the majority of the common population of Lebennin and Anfalas.[file:73]

aspect.en: Half-grown trolls, not yet at full size but already dangerous — clumsier and more reckless than their elders, often driven from a lair to fend for themselves. Toward travellers: easier prey than a full troll, but a pack of them is no small peril.

lore.en: Half-grown Trolls, not yet at full size or strength but already dangerous — clumsier and more reckless than their elders, and often driven from a lair to fend for themselves. Easier prey than a full-grown Troll, but a pack of them is no small peril.

aspect.en: A short, sturdy pony with wide hooves for soft ground and powerful lungs, mostly grey with a long silky mane — bred for wet, boggy country. Toward travellers: a hardy, sure-footed mount well-suited to marsh and fen.

lore.en: Also called the Perroch-i-Lin, the Marsh Pony is a short, sturdy beast with relatively wide hooves and powerful lungs. Most are grey, and all have a long, silky mane.

aspect.en: Dúnedain rangers who watch the wild northern lands and shadow the movements of the Witch-king's armies — secret guardians of the depopulated North. Toward travellers: grim, unseen protectors; they challenge strangers but defend the innocent and aid the worthy in need.

lore.en: Dúnedain rangers monitoring the movements of the Witch-king's armies.

aspect.en: Orc scouts and Mannish soldiers ranging out from the border towers of Angmar. Toward travellers: hostile patrols of an evil realm — they hunt intruders and challenge any who cross their watch.

lore.en: Orc scouts and Mannish soldiers operating from border towers like Cargash.

aspect.en: A deliberate trap set to kill or maim — a concealed pit, deadfall, snare, spring-spike or worse, laid by brigands, guardians or the builders of a stronghold. Toward travellers: easy to blunder into and hard to spot until sprung; watch the ground near ruins, lairs and guarded places.

lore.en: A deliberate trap set to kill or maim — a concealed pit, deadfall, snare, spring-spike or worse, laid by brigands, guardians or the builders of some stronghold. Easy to blunder into and hard to spot until it is sprung.

aspect.en: A spring where water rises from the ground — a welcome find for the thirsty, though some run foul, mineral-tainted or scalding, and a few are held sacred or guarded by what dwells near. Toward travellers: usually a blessing on the road, but taste with care, and beware what may watch over it.

lore.en: A spring where water rises from the ground — a welcome find for the thirsty, though some run foul, mineral-tainted or scalding, and a few are held sacred or guarded by what dwells near them.

aspect.en: A coffle of captives driven under armed guard toward the markets or some master's labour, herded by hard-eyed keepers — the guards watchful and brutal, the slaves broken but alert for any chance to flee. Toward travellers: the guards are violent and suspicious; the slaves may beg aid or seize a chance to break free.

lore.en: A coffle of slaves driven under armed guard — captives bound for the markets or the labor of some master, herded along the road by hard-eyed keepers. The guards are watchful and brutal; the slaves, broken but always alert for a chance to flee.

aspect.en: Lawless men of the road and wild — robbers, deserters, broken soldiers and hired ruffians who prey on travellers and lone farms, banding where order is weak and scattering before real force. Toward travellers: a direct danger; they demand toll or plunder at knife-point but break before a strong, armed party.

lore.en: Lawless men of the road and the wild — robbers, deserters, broken soldiers and hired ruffians who prey on travellers and isolated farms. They band together where order is weak, demand toll or plunder at knife-point, and scatter before any real strength of arms.

aspect.en: A huge, weasel-like predator — fierce, restless and ravenous, killing almost anything it can overpower, even boars and small bears. An agile climber that dens in hollow trees, with a keen nose. Toward travellers: won't seek out people, but is reckless and aggressive and dangerous if it does.

lore.en: Huge relative of the common weasel (S. "Carlûmon", pl. "Cerlymyn"), a fierce, irrational and hyperactive creature that must eat constantly. Totally carnivorous (foraging nuts and berries only when starving), it kills anything it can disable, even Small Bears and Wild Boars. Acrobatic and an excellent climber, it dens in hollow trees and has a keen nose and fair vision.

aspect.en: A great wingless cold-drake of the northern mountains whose breath is killing frost rather than fire; it lairs among high snows and frozen caves, leaving men and beasts rimed and dead in its wake. Toward travellers: a named horror of the far peaks whose very breath freezes the life from the living.

lore.en: Gondring, a great cold-drake of the northern mountains — a wingless dragon whose breath is killing frost rather than fire. It lairs among high snows and frozen caves, and its passing leaves men and beasts rimed and dead.

aspect.en: A lone traveller on a journey of faith or penance, bound for some shrine or vow far from home — footsore and single-minded, trusting to charity and to the protection their purpose is thought to grant. Toward travellers: harmless and devout, glad of kindness and company and no threat.

lore.en: A lone traveller on a journey of faith or penance, bound for some shrine, holy place or vow far from home. Footsore and single-minded, pilgrims trust to the charity of those they meet and to the protection their purpose is thought to grant.

aspect.en: The Dark Lord in hidden guise, lurking in the hill-fortress of Dol Guldur — a radiating source of fear and corruption that breeds orcs, trolls, spiders and fell beasts at the dark heart of southern Mirkwood. Toward travellers: an overwhelming, malevolent power; his very presence is dread, and his servants hunt all who approach.

lore.en: Sauron in his guise as the Necromancer, occupying Dol Guldur since the 12th century T.A., radiating fear and corruption, breeding Orcs, trolls, spiders and fell beasts, and acting as the dark center of Southern Mirkwood.

aspect.en: A primitive woodland folk akin to the Wild-men, dwelling in the dark forests of a remote peninsula — secretive, using treacherous woods and coasts to stay beyond Dúnadan rule and keep their own ways. Toward travellers: shy and elusive, shunning outsiders; wary in their woods but not aggressors unless threatened.

lore.en: A relatively primitive folk akin to Drúedain, inhabiting the dark woods of the Rast Vorn peninsula; they are secretive, use the treacherous forest and coasts to remain largely outside Dúnadan control and maintain their own customs.[file:31]

aspect.en: A roving band of orc soldiery under a snaga or larger goblin, watching the roads, passes and borders of the Enemy's lands for intruders, runaway slaves or prey. Quarrelsome and cruel, moving by night and shunning the sun. Toward travellers: hostile on sight — they hunt, harry and kill.

lore.en: A patrol of Orcs sweeping the roads, passes and borders of the Enemy's lands — a handful of soldiery under a snaga or larger goblin, watching for intruders, escaped slaves or prey. Quarrelsome and cruel, they move by night where they can and shun the open sun.

aspect.en: Blood-sucking worms of still, sluggish water that fasten unseen to anything warm-blooded wading the shallows. Toward travellers: a foul nuisance of fen and marsh — in bad waters thick enough to weaken a wading beast.

lore.en: Blood-sucking worms of still and sluggish water, fastening unseen to any warm-blooded thing that wades the shallows. A nuisance of fen and marsh, and in foul waters they gather thick enough to weaken a wading beast.

aspect.en: Large river otters with flattened, sharp-crested tails, moving in small daytime family groups along rivers and denning in banks and sandbars. Prized for their pelts and now protected and scarce. Toward travellers: shy and water-bound — little threat to people.

lore.en: Larger than common otters, with flattened, sharp-crested tails. Travel in small daytime groups feeding on fish eggs, small aquatic mammals and birds; den in sandbars or riverbanks, bearing only 1-2 young a year. Their large profile and valuable pelts make them endangered; protected by hunting bans across northwestern Endor, notably Gondor.

aspect.en: Traders plying goods between towns and lands — cloth, metalwork, salt, wine and small luxuries — with a laden pony, pack or guarded wagon; shrewd, talkative, carrying news as readily as wares. Toward travellers: welcoming and useful for goods and news, canny in a bargain but no threat.

lore.en: Traders plying their goods between towns and lands — cloth, metalwork, salt, wine and small luxuries, with a laden pony, a pack or a guarded wagon. Shrewd and talkative, they carry news as readily as wares and know the roads and prices of half a kingdom.

aspect.en: A hardy, gregarious deer with a long low body and large branched antlers borne by both sexes, ranging from white to black but mostly grey or silver; females move in great herds, males alone or in small groups. Hunted by wolves, bears and above all Men. Toward travellers: harmless; a familiar sight on the cold northern ranges, herded and hunted by the local peoples.

lore.en: The Losrandir is a hardy, gregarious Deer with a long, low profile and large antlers. They come in many colors—everything from white to jet black—but most are grey or silver. Unlike those of other Deer, the low forward tine of its antlers is branched. Both males and females bear antlers, although those of the female are usually smaller. Female Losrandír (aka "Lesrandír") move in large herds while males travel in small groups or, in some cases, alone. Wolves and Bears prey on weaker individuals, but the Losrandir's greatest natural enemy is undoubtedly Man. The Lossoth of northwestern Middle-earth and the Urd of the northeast hunt the graceful creature for its fur, meat, and utility as a beast of burden.

aspect.en: Ancient demons of fire and shadow — among Morgoth's first and mightiest servants, immortal and singular. Towering, wreathed in flame and darkness, wielding fiery whip and sword; the Balrog of Moria slew Dwarf-kings and emptied the city before Gandalf destroyed it. Toward travellers: catastrophic and all but unkillable — a force to flee, not fight.

lore.en: Evil Spirits of Fire (S. "Demons of Might"), among Morgoth's first allies in the early days of Arda; immortal and singular. The Balrog of Moria (Durin's Bane), perhaps the last of his kind, was roused by deep-delving Dwarves, slew two Dwarf-kings and drove the rest from Moria, and was finally vanquished by Gandalf. Its First Age kin Gothmog and the White Balrog Lungorthin are long gone.

aspect.en: The chief predator of the settled lands between the Misty and Blue Mountains — unlike the grey wolf, a vicious, tireless hunter that kills for sport, preys on sheep and does not fear Men, readily attacking lone folk or small groups. Toward travellers: bold and aggressive, a real danger even to armed parties, countered only by sheep-hounds and watchfulness.

lore.en: Chief predator (S. Draucaran, Q. Carnanarmo) of the settled reaches between the Misty Mountains and the Blue Mountains, particularly common in southern Eriador from Cardolan south to the Belegaer. Unlike the Grey Wolf it is a vicious, tireless hunter prone to kill for sport, preying chiefly on sheep and unafraid of Men, readily attacking lone individuals or small groups. Sheep Hounds have proved an effective counter to it.

aspect.en: A Sindar-led Elf-haven at the mouth of the Morthond, famed for white swan-ships and as guardians of a sacred wood — Sindar shipwrights and captains over Silvan hunters and fishers, building the fairest ships of southern Gondor. Toward travellers: courteous sea-elves of a hidden haven, gracious to friends and to the worthy.

lore.en: A Sindar-led Elf-haven at the mouth of the Morthond, famed for its white swan-ships and as guardians of Eryn Laegol; the Sindar provide shipwrights, captains and leaders while Silvan Elves form most of the common folk, hunters and fishers. Closely allied with the Princes of Belfalas, they build the most beautiful ships in Southern Gondor.

aspect.en: Owls of wood, ruin and barn, hunting silently by night for mice and small birds — their calls carrying far in the dark and read by country folk as luck or ill omen; by day they roost hidden in hollow trees and rafters. Toward travellers: harmless, a silent night-shape and a cry the superstitious read for omens.

lore.en: Owls of wood, ruin and barn, hunting silently by night for mice, voles and small birds. Their calls carry far in the dark, and country folk read luck or ill omen in them; by day they roost hidden in hollow trees and rafters.

aspect.en: A large brown deer of northern Eriador and the cool northwest — one of the few deer in which both sexes bear antlers — moving in immense herds, thousands strong, across open country and broken woodland, some ranging far into the North. Toward travellers: harmless; a vast migrating herd is a stirring sight on the open lands.

lore.en: The Caru (Du. "Elk") is a large brown Deer commonly found in northern Eriador, but ranging throughout the cooler parts of northwestern Middle-earth. It is the only Deer species, save the Losrandir, in which both the males and females sport antlers. Caru travel in huge herds of one to twenty thousand and range over vast areas of open country or broken woodlands. Feeding on grass and other tundra plants in the summer, some roam well into the Far North.

aspect.en: The oldest and commonest dragon-breed, ancestor of all others — winged or wingless, fireless but vast and cunning, haunting northern mountain caverns; the Grey Dragons of the Ered Mithrin are of this kind. Toward travellers: an ancient armoured worm, deadly even without fire — a peril to a whole realm.

lore.en: Cold-drakes (Q. "Helkaloki") are the most common and oldest breed of Dragon, from which all others descend; wingless or winged, they haunt northern mountain caverns and are the Grey Dragons (Sintanguleki) of the Ered Mithrin.

aspect.en: A striking lichen forming pale, intricate patterns on rock and old trunks in the deepest shadows of Mirkwood, used by lore-masters as a marker of deep shadow and in rare dream- and vision-draughts. Toward travellers: harmless; a curiosity prized by herb-lore and a sign of the forest's darkest reaches.

lore.en: A striking lichen that forms pale, intricate patterns on rocks and old trunks in the deepest shadowed parts of Mirkwood. It is used by lore-masters and alchemists as a marker of deep shadow and in rare draughts tied to dreams and visions.

aspect.en: A catch-all for the lesser wild beasts of a region — the mixed creatures of wood, field and hill a traveller might glimpse or stumble upon. Toward travellers: most flee from people, but hunger, season or injury can make any of them bold.

lore.en: A catch-all for the lesser wild beasts of a region — the mixed mammals and creatures of wood, field and hill a traveller might glimpse or stumble upon. Most flee from Men, but hunger, season or wounds can make any of them bold or dangerous.

aspect.en: Feral dogs running in packs through the wilds and the fringes of settlement — scavenging carrion and pulling down small or weakened prey, cowardly alone but bold in numbers. Toward travellers: a persistent nuisance and a danger to the lone or weak when the pack grows bold.

lore.en: Feral dogs running in packs through the wilds and the fringes of settlement, scavenging carrion and pulling down small or weakened prey. Cowardly alone but bold in numbers, they are a persistent nuisance to herders and travellers.

aspect.en: An oversized blood-drinking bat of the southern and eastern lands that lands on sleeping beasts and men to feed; its bite is scarcely felt until it has gorged, and a colony can leave livestock weak and bloodless. Toward travellers: a stealthy night-feeder on the sleeping — post a watch where they haunt.

lore.en: An oversized blood-drinking bat of the southern and eastern lands that descends on sleeping beasts and men to feed. Its bite is scarcely felt until the creature is gorged, and a colony can leave livestock weak and bloodless.

aspect.en: Cricket-like marsh insects of the northern wetlands, named for their endless night-cry of "neek-breek, neek-breek." Little more than a nuisance — though they will infest and devour unguarded grain, flour or waybread. Toward travellers: a sleepless din, and a threat to loosely-wrapped food stores.

lore.en: Noisy, cricketlike insects that are found in marshy areas in the northerly regions of Endor (e.g., Arthedain), Neekerbreekers are little more than a major nuisance. Their name is derived from their noisy, incessant night cry. Those experienced with and accustomed to travel in these regions soon learn to tolerate the sound of Neekerbreekers, but travellers carrying dried grains, flour, or waybread are well advised to keep these supplies tightly wrapped in areas where the hideous "neek-breek, neek-breek!" can be heard, since Neekerbreekers have been known to infest and devour such food. Neekerbreekers are found in particularly foul swamps. Gigantic relatives of the mosquito, these carnivores prefer solid meat. So, while it does not suck blood, a Neekerbreeker will appropriate small chunks of a man's flesh. Any wound inflicted by a Neekerbreeker has a chance of being infected with Yellow Rheum, a 0 level illness.

aspect.en: A place of the Drúedain — a carved Púkel-stone, hidden camp or forest shrine marked by their watchful guardian-statues. Toward travellers: easily overlooked and best left undisturbed; the Wild-men guard their places, and their statues may be more than stone.

lore.en: A place of the Drúedain (Woses) — a carved Púkel-stone, hidden camp or forest shrine, marked by their watchful guardian-statues. Easily overlooked and best left undisturbed by outsiders.

aspect.en: Featherless, reptilian winged monsters that roost in the hills near Dol Guldur, bred or drawn to the Necromancer's service and later borne by the Nazgûl; their shadow and reek bring terror before they strike. Toward travellers: a horror of the sky near the dark hill — dread goes before them, and they hunt at evil command.

lore.en: The winged fell beasts that roost in the Emyn Guldur near Dol Guldur — featherless, reptilian flyers bred or drawn to the Necromancer's service and later borne by the Nazgûl. Their shadow and reek bring terror before ever they strike.

aspect.en: Water-loving cats of the eastern marshes, with semi-webbed paws — strong swimmers that flip fish from the water and also take birds, shellfish and frogs, hiding mottled among the reeds; kittens can be tamed as one-person pets. Toward travellers: shy and water-bound, no real threat to people.

lore.en: Aquatic cats most common in the marshes along the eastern shores of the Sea of Rhûn and in the Wetwang (Nindalf) in Ithilien. With no dislike of water and semi-webbed paws, they swim well and flip fish from the water, supplementing their diet with birds, shellfish and amphibians. Mottled grey-brown fur hides them among reeds; kittens can be tamed but stay one-person pets.

aspect.en: The smaller, common cousin of the war-mûmak — a true elephant with pillar legs, great ears, a grasping trunk and long tusks, eating hundreds of pounds of foliage a day. Toward travellers: a placid browser, but a frightened or angered one is immensely dangerous; some peoples ride or work them.

lore.en: The Andamunda (Q. "Elephant"; pl. "Andamundar"; lit. "Long-snouted") is the smaller and more numerous cousin of the famous Mûmak. Like all its cousins, it has thick, pillarlike legs and flat, padded feet; loose skin and large ears provide heat regulation, enabling it to adapt to a variety of ecosystems. Its most notable feature is its trunk: an elongated nose and upper lip that serves as both a sensory organ and a prehensile grasping tool, used to smell, gather food, drink, and as a weapon in combat. Its pair of long tusks serve primarily as digging tools (it subsists on roots, shoots, twigs, fruit, leaves), a typical Andamunda eating about 400 pounds of food a day. Always active except for rest periods at night and a midday break, it roams in a constant search for security and food; its plodding belies its strength as a swift, agile runner that can run down and gore a foe. Unlike the Mûmak, it has a slightly humped back and one (vs. two or three) fingerlike extension at the base of its trunk, plus a gland to secrete scented waste. Like Mûmakil, females travel in herds led by an elder matriarch, bearing one offspring (after 21 months gestation) and raising the calf for 24-30 months. Domesticated by various cultures, used less than Mûmakil as riding animals but much easier to tame.

aspect.en: Huge, stupid creatures bred by Morgoth in mockery of Ents, as tough and dull as the stone they were made from and hating all living things; most kinds turn to stone in daylight, for they were made in darkness. Toward travellers: immensely strong and murderous by night, survivable mainly by holding out until sunrise.

lore.en: Bred by Morgoth in mockery of Ents, Trolls are as tough and stupid as the stone from which they were made. Some feel they are related to Giants. In any case, Trolls hate all other creatures, a legacy of Morgoth's dark touch. Normal Trolls are divided into several types (based on their location): Hill, Cave, Snow, and Stone-trolls. The latter is the most common group. These types all revert to the stone of their substance when exposed to the light of day, for they were created in Darkness and the Sun can unmake them. Physical Character: They are huge and immensely strong, with thick bodies and limbs. Their tough hides have an inconsistent quality; many have overlapping scales and some have body hair. Various shades of brown, green, or grey hide, with black or brown eyes. They have black blood. Average endurance. 9 to 11 feet. Variable lifespan; hundreds of years. Trolls do not understand fear. Their vision is the same as that of Orcs. Sunlight. When exposed to the natural light of day they turn to stone. Trolls live in order to play and eat. To them play means killing and pillaging, and eating means fresh meat - raw or cooked - or jelly made from innards.

aspect.en: A seven-foot snake of the dry western Harad hills, named "snare" for its method — it lashes out a barbed tail to coil round a limb, the barbs delivering a paralysing venom through the skin, then constricts its immobilised prey. Toward travellers: a dangerous ambusher whose whipping, barbed tail can entangle and poison.

lore.en: The Zamka (pl. "Zamkavi") is common to the dry hills of western Harad. Its name translates as "snare," and is derived from this snake's method of attack. The Zamka whips its tail out like a lash and coils about a limb or appendage. The snake's long (7') body is lined with small barbs along each side. The barbs are coated with a poisonous secretion which enters through the skin of its victim. This (7th lvl) muscle poison essentially paralyzes the prey (duration = 20 minutes per ten points of RR failure). When its venom takes effect—in forty-five seconds—the serpent will move to constrict its prey. Once the victim is dead, the Zamka remains with the corpse until time and weather has softened it, then begins its feast. Other animals steer well clear of any kill it guards. Note: the Entangle Table is used with any critical indicating a poisoning; it aims at bare skin, will attack while the victim is moving, and continues until movement ceases.

aspect.en: Footpads, cutpurses and smugglers working the towns, fairs and trade-roads — moving stolen goods and contraband, slipping tolls and gates, and lightening the purses of the unwary. Toward travellers: quick-fingered and quick to vanish, a danger to your goods and gold rather than your life — but dangerous if cornered.

lore.en: Footpads, cutpurses and smugglers who work the towns, fairs and trade-roads, moving stolen goods and contraband, slipping past tolls and gates, and lightening the purses of the unwary. Quick-fingered and quicker to vanish, they answer to whoever pays.

aspect.en: A large predatory lizard of the southern wilds, big enough to threaten dogs, livestock and children — quick over short bursts, ambushing prey and defending its lair with snapping jaws and lashing tail. Toward travellers: a real danger to the small and the careless near its lair, and dangerous if cornered.

lore.en: A large predatory lizard of the southern wilds, big enough to threaten dogs, livestock and children. Quick over short distances, it ambushes prey and defends its lair with snapping jaws and lashing tail.

aspect.en: A seldom-seen grey-and-purple bat of remote Mirkwood that hunts night-birds, large spiders and rodents — the larger ones able to fell a small bear — and sucks the blood and soft flesh of its prey. Toward travellers: a rare but dangerous blood-drinker of the deep forest night; the great ones can threaten a lone sleeper.

lore.en: Seldom-seen, the grey and purple Great Bat is found in remoter parts of Mirkwood. Little is known of its habits. It eats night-flying birds (e.g., Owls), large spiders, and various rodents, although larger individuals have been known to fell a small bear. The Great Bat sucks blood (always a tempting notion to those who dislike bats, even the small insectivorous kind) from its victims, and feeds on the softer flesh of its prey.

aspect.en: A lone Dwarf or small party searching the roots of the Blue Mountains for fresh seams of iron, coal or precious metal — secretive about finds, ranging the high valleys with pick, lamp and a keen eye for stone. Toward travellers: gruff and close-mouthed about their work, but no threat to honest folk.

lore.en: A lone Dwarf or small party searching the roots of the Blue Mountains for fresh seams of iron, coal or precious metal. Secretive about their finds, prospectors range the high valleys with pick, lamp and a keen eye for the lie of the stone.

aspect.en: Mountain clans of the White Mountains living above the treeline in simple groupings — semi-nomadic goat-herds and, on the coast, fisherfolk — who have largely shunned Gondorian ways and keep their ancient traditions. Toward travellers: insular and proud, suspicious of outsiders but not hostile without cause.

lore.en: Mountain clans of the White Mountains living above the timberline in primitive groupings; semi-nomadic goat shepherds and fisherfolk on the coasts (Dunir of Andrast), they have largely avoided cultural contact with Gondor and still honor ancient Daen traditions.[file:73]

aspect.en: Workings cut into hill and mountain for metal and stone — iron, tin, copper, silver, gems or mithril — marked by spoil-heaps, smelters and guarded ore-roads. Toward travellers: a place of industry and guarded wealth, and the deeper delvings can wake older perils.

lore.en: Workings cut into hill and mountain for metal and stone — iron, tin, copper, lead, silver, gems or mithril, hewn in shaft and gallery. Spoil-heaps, smelters and guarded ore-roads mark the diggings, and the deeper delvings can wake older perils.

aspect.en: Wild rabbits and hares of field and woodland edge — quick, plentiful and always watchful, bolting for cover at the least alarm. Toward travellers: harmless; chiefly of interest as game for the pot.

lore.en: Wild rabbits and hares of field, down and woodland edge — quick, prolific and ever-watchful. A staple of hunters, hawks and foxes, they bolt for cover at the least alarm.

aspect.en: The noblest horses of Middle-earth, descended from the steed of the Vala of the hunt — most white or dappled-grey, long-lived and supremely strong, understanding speech and bearing only the worthy. Toward travellers: peerless mounts of kings; they answer only to those they accept and will not suffer an unworthy rider.

lore.en: These Horses are among the most noble of the Endorian beasts. They were unknown as a breed before ca. T.A. 2545, the approximate date that the first breeding herd was fully established in Rohan by Eorl the Young; however, individual Mearas were to be found in Middle-earth before that date. They are commonly (and correctly) believed to be the descendants of Nahar, the Steed of Oromë, as are the Elven Horses. The progenitor of the breed in Rohan was Felaróf, who was white; such was his strength as an ancestor that most of his descendants are white or dappled gray. All Mearas, regardless of color, share Felaróf's other characteristics: they understand human speech, can be ridden without saddle or bridle (although they will tolerate such devices if needed), and live to a great age (eighty years is not unusual). Famous individuals include Felaróf (captured by Léod of the Éothéod, who named him Mansbane before Eorl renamed him), Shadowfax (Gandalf's steed, chief of the Mearas in Théoden's time), and Snowmane (Steed of King Théoden, who fell at the Pelennor Fields).

aspect.en: Great evil wolves of the North — larger and more cunning than common wolves, bound in malice to the orcs they often bear into battle; they hunt in savage packs, share a crude speech and gather at the Enemy's call. Toward travellers: a deadly, intelligent pack-hunter and servant of darkness, a grave danger on wild roads, above all by night.

lore.en: Great evil wolves of the North, larger and more cunning than common wolves and bound in malice to the Orcs, whom they often bear into battle. They hunt in savage packs, share a crude speech of their own, and gather at the Enemy's call.

aspect.en: Dense, thorny bramble and briar that chokes wood-edge, ruin and waste — a tangle that tears clothes and flesh and slows any passage; in old or tainted places it grows rank and almost clutching, as if with a will of its own. Toward travellers: a painful, slowing barrier — and in dark places, a hedge that seems to grasp at those who push through.

lore.en: Dense, thorny bramble and briar that chokes wood-edge, ruin and waste — a tangle that tears clothes and flesh and slows any passage. In some old or tainted places the briars grow rank and clutching, almost as if with a will of their own.

aspect.en: A dragon of the first rank — ancient, immense and terrible, often fire-breathing and wing-borne, with a guileful tongue and a hoard to match its years; few remain, and the coming of one is a calamity for whole kingdoms. Toward travellers: not a danger but a doom — to face one is to face the ruin of realms.

lore.en: A dragon of the first rank — ancient, immense and terrible, often fire-breathing and wing-borne, with a guileful tongue and a hoard to match its age. Few remain, and the coming of one is a calamity for kingdoms, not merely travellers.

aspect.en: The common wild wolf, found across Middle-earth — near-black in warm lands, near-white in the North — thickly furred and deeply social, hunting deer and sheep in cooperative family packs; mated pairs stay together for life. Toward travellers: wary of armed folk, but a pack is dangerous to the lone or weak, especially in hard times.

lore.en: Powerful, muscular dog (S. Draugwath, Q. Mistanarmo) with a thick coat and bushy tail, ranging all over Middle-earth and varying from near-black in warm locales to almost white in the North. Exceptionally social, living in family groups or packs that hunt cooperatively, favouring Deer and Sheep in warm climes and Caru or Losrandir in cooler ones, with rodents, fish and crustaceans besides. Mated pairs stay together for life and rarely fight over mates.

aspect.en: A place of the Dunlendings — a hill-fort, clan-hall, standing stone or burial cairn of the old folk of Dunland. Toward travellers: jealously guarded by wary clans who resent trespass; approach uninvited at your risk.

lore.en: A site of the Dunlendings — a hill-fort, clan-hall, standing stone or burial cairn of the old folk of Dunland. Wary of strangers, the clans guard their places jealously and resent trespass.

aspect.en: Highly intelligent, long-lived birds aligned with good — said to be messengers of the keeper of the dead and linked to fate and foresight; the Ravens of Erebor long counselled Durin's Dwarves, and most can speak the tongues of the Free Peoples. Toward travellers: wise and watchful, a possible ally and bearer of news to the worthy.

lore.en: Ravens are among the more intelligent birds to be found in Middle-earth. Not as noble nor as wise as the Great Eagles, Ravens are nevertheless on the side of good, unlike all too many of their lesser Corvidae cousins. They are reputedly the messengers of the Vala Namo (Mandos) and are associated with Fate and Prescience. The Ravens of Erebor befriended and counselled the Dwarves of the Line of Durin during the Third Age. These noble birds live a long time: Roac of Erebor lived past 150 years of age. Brilliant and somewhat enchanted, most Ravens can speak the tongues of the Free Peoples (or at least of Men and Elves; the tongue of the Dwarves is too secret and that of the Ents too lengthy for ravens to learn). Conjurers have long sought out the foreknowledge of Ravens.

aspect.en: Garrison troops and militia of Calenardhon — Gondor's grassland province before Rohan — holding its forts, fords and roads against orcs and Dunlending raiders out of the hills. Toward travellers: disciplined king's soldiers, allies to the lawful and watchful of strangers on a raided frontier.

lore.en: Soldiers of Calenardhon, the great grassland province of Gondor before it was granted to the Rohirrim — garrison troops and militia holding its forts, fords and roads against Orcs and Dunlending raiders out of the hills.

aspect.en: Large black mountain birds that nest in colonies on sheer cliffs and, unusually, hunt cooperatively — banding together to mob and drive large or wounded creatures off a precipice, then feasting below. Toward travellers: a real danger to the injured, or to anyone caught on a cliff-edge in their territory.

lore.en: The Cliff Buzzard is a large, black-feathered bird of the mountains. It builds its nest on inaccessible cliffs. Often several pairs will nest in the same area, behavior more typical of the Corvidae (crowlike birds) than of the Raptors (Hawks and so on). Cliff Buzzards exhibit a great deal of intelligence (for birds) and will cooperate in hunting. They will band together to mob some large creature and drive it over a cliff so that they may all feast together on the shattered body. Any wounded creature, no matter what its size, may be subject to the unwanted attentions of the Cliff Buzzards. They are most common on the southern slopes of the White Mountains.

aspect.en: A savage, wain-riding Easterling people who roam the grasslands in search of plunder. Toward travellers: hostile and predatory — raiders who fall upon the unwary rather than parley.

lore.en: A savage, wain-riding Easterling people who wander the grasslands in search of plunder.

aspect.en: Huge war-dogs, often mistaken for Wargs but truly only overlarge wolves bred and trained for battle — bolder, fiercer and more cunning than wild wolves, fielded in numbers as trackers and harriers and even ridden by orcs in the North. Toward travellers: trained killers loosed in packs, a serious danger where the Enemy or war-bands field them.

lore.en: Huge dogs (S. Ormaraka, aka Yelmaraka), often mistaken for Wargs, bred and trained for combat and frequently fielded in numbers as trackers, scouts or to harass enemy armies. The War-wolves of Waw serve as combat units, while those of Angmar are used as mounts by Orcish raiders and Orc-lords. They look like merely overlarge Wolves, which is true, but they are bolder, far more violent and much more cunning.

aspect.en: A low, broad-leafed herb of damp meadows and marsh-margins; infusions are said to steady the nerves, lift the heart and give courage before battle or a long road, a favourite of Northmen healers. Toward travellers: harmless and heartening, a herb worth carrying for hard journeys.

lore.en: A low, broad-leafed herb of damp meadows and marshy margins. Infusions are said to steady the nerves, cheer the heart and give courage before battle or long journeys, making it a favorite of Northmen healers.

aspect.en: Long, snakelike fish of muddy rivers, meres and estuaries — night-hunters that hide in weed and silt by day; slippery and hard to hold, the larger ones biting sharply, and some sea-kinds growing alarmingly big. Toward travellers: little real threat — a nuisance to anglers and a startle to waders, save for the rare giant kind.
