lore.en: Long, snakelike fish of muddy rivers, meres and estuaries, hunting by night and hiding in weed and silt by day. Slippery and hard to hold, the larger ones bite sharply and some salt-water kinds grow alarmingly big.

aspect.en: Ancient tree-like beings, the shepherds of the forests — vast, slow and immensely strong, with long memory and longer patience. Toward travellers: usually aloof and unhurried, no threat to those who mean the trees no harm — but terrible in anger against those who do.

lore.en: Ancient tree-like beings, shepherds of the forests, also known as Onodrim.

aspect.en: A bright green, flightless bird like a long-legged goose — an excellent swimmer living on fish and shellfish, fleeing predators with surprising clumsy speed but bravely defending its eggs in nesting season. Toward travellers: harmless and timid, except when guarding a nest.

lore.en: A Golodo is a bright green, moderately large, flightless bird, rather like a large goose on stilts. Excellent swimmers, they subsist primarily on fish, crustaceans, and shellfish. Golodos gather in large flocks during the breeding season in early summer, traveling in small groups during the rest of the year. Golodos will immediately flee the scent of any predator with surprising, if ungainly speed, except during the nesting season, when they will bravely defend their eggs. Given to snapping up carrion, Golodos enjoy the taste of meat; however, they will eat anything, since they are poor hunters.

aspect.en: Orc scouts ranging ahead of larger forces or on a raid of their own — stealthier and warier than common orcs, spying the land and the strength of foes and slipping back to report rather than fight in the open. Toward travellers: dangerous spies; meeting them may mean a larger force soon knows you are there.

lore.en: Orc scouts ranging ahead of larger forces or out on a raid of their own, spying the land, the roads and the strength of their foes. Stealthier and warier than common Orcs, they avoid open battle and slip back to report what they have seen.

aspect.en: The lesser lizards, skinks and snakes that scuttle through warm rock, scrub and ruin — harmless to all but insects and each other. Toward travellers: no threat; a sign of dry, sun-warmed country.

lore.en: The lesser lizards, skinks and snakes that scuttle through warm rock, scrub and ruin. Harmless to all but insects and each other, they are signs of dry, sun-warmed country.

aspect.en: Big, brutish trolls of the highlands and broken hill-country — the Trollshaws, Ettenmoors and Misty Mountains — stronger and hardier than Men but dull-witted, lairing in caves and ruins and raiding lonely roads by night; older kinds fear the stone-turning sun. Toward travellers: a deadly night-ambush on hill-roads, best escaped until dawn.

lore.en: Big, brutish Trolls of the highlands and broken hill-country, met among the crags of the Trollshaws, the Coldfells, the Ettenmoors and the Misty Mountains. Stronger and hardier than Men but dull-witted, they lair in caves and ruins and raid lonely roads by night — and the older breeds must beware the sun that turns them to stone.

aspect.en: A rust-brown banded water-snake of still pools, marshes and lakes, three to five feet long; it rarely strikes in water — victims are usually on land when they cross its "runs," where it bites with startling speed and a bleeding venom. Toward travellers: a hidden danger along marsh-paths rather than in open water.

lore.en: The Nathrach (pl. "Nethraich") is an aquatic snake that resides in relatively placid or stagnant pools, marshes, and lakes. Brown bands surround its rust-colored body, which typically measures three to five feet in length. Contrary to popular belief, this serpent does not normally strike in water; most victims are on dry land or a marsh island when they stray into a snake run. These snakes only attack when their "runs" are encountered, and then it bites with astounding quickness. A Nathrach's critical strike is accompanied by a muscle poison that causes bleeding, bruises, and swelling (double all these effects on this and subsequent criticals). The venom is not very toxic (level 2) but is designed to stun small rodents. The Arnathrach (pl. "Ernaithrach"), or Royal Nathrach, is a much larger cousin that inhabits the brackish waters near the coasts.

aspect.en: A lone Dúnadan on the road — one of the long-lived, far-wandering Men of Westernesse, abroad on some errand of their own; grave, courteous and watchful. Toward travellers: a doughty, honourable companion who keeps their lineage and purpose close.

lore.en: A lone Dúnadan upon the road — one of the long-lived, far-wandering Men of Westernesse, abroad on some errand of their own. Grave, courteous and watchful, such a traveller makes a doughty companion and keeps their lineage and purpose close.

aspect.en: Brave, hardy foresters and horse-herders with strong warrior traditions. Toward travellers: tough but honourable folk, wary of strangers though not aggressors.

lore.en: Brave, resilient foresters and horse-herders with strong warrior traditions.

aspect.en: The giant of freshwater fish, growing up to eighteen feet and armoured with rows of bony plates; normally docile, feeding on the bottom, but it will thrash and ram river-craft if its lair is disturbed. Prized for meat and roe. Toward travellers: harmless unless disturbed, when its sheer size can upset a boat.

lore.en: The granddaddy of all freshwater fish, the Sturgeon grows up to 18' long in still waters. It has a scaly skin, which is protected by five rows of bony scutes along its sides. Normally very docile, one of these formidable creatures will only attack if its lair is disturbed. Then, it thrashes about angrily, perhaps ramming or upsetting any nearby river craft. Grey and silver, the Sturgeon resides in shallow seas and rivers, feeding on the worms, mollusks, crustaceans, and small fish that live on or near the bottom. They are prized for their meat and their exceedingly tasty eggs.

aspect.en: A clever, lively marsh-and-shore crow, glossy black with an iridescent green wing-patch. Tameable even as adults, they make fine homing messengers, though like all their kin they are easily distracted by anything shiny. Toward travellers: harmless and curious; sometimes kept as pets or message-bearers.

lore.en: A lively, intelligent bird of the marshes and shores, the Green-winged Crow can be tamed even as an adult. They make effective messengers, able to find their way home from any direction within a 75-100 mile radius. However, like most of the Corvidae, they are attracted and distracted by shiny objects. With their shiny black plumage marked distinctively on the "shoulder" of the wing with a patch of iridescent green, these crows make attractive pets.

aspect.en: A voracious giant freshwater mink (50-80 lbs) of marshes and waterways — usually a lone hunter, but in spring it gangs into mating-mobs that attack anything in their path. Toward travellers: a savage water-weasel; little threat singly, but a spring mob is dangerous near the water.

lore.en: Voracious freshwater predator, much larger than common mink (50-80 lbs). Most common in the Wetwang (Nindalf) near Ithilien, otherwise in north-central Middle-earth always near water. Hunts alone but mobs in early-spring mating gangs of 7-12, attacking anything in its path. Its thick, glossy, waterproof pelt fetches 6-15 gp.

aspect.en: Disaffected soldiers, desperate peasants and local rogues haunting the roads and ruins of the depopulated frontier, caring for nothing but what they can steal. Toward travellers: a direct danger — robber bands that prey on the lone and the laden.

lore.en: Disaffected soldiers, plague-maddened peasants and local rogues haunting the roads and ruins, turning the depopulated frontier into a patchwork of robber bands unconcerned with Gondor or Sauron beyond what they can steal.[file:37]

aspect.en: A tall, straight, pale-barked tree prized by Elven and Dúnedain shipwrights — its wood light but strong and good at holding fastenings, ideal for masts, spars and planking. Toward travellers: harmless; a valuable timber and a sign of ship-building country.

lore.en: Gwingyrn is a tall, straight, pale-barked tree prized by Elven and Dúnedain shipwrights. Its wood is light but strong and holds fastenings well, making it ideal for masts, spars and planking.

aspect.en: Orcs trained to hunt by scent and sign, set on the trail of escaped thralls, spies or travellers — tenacious and savage, the best able to follow a cold trail for days and rarely giving up a quarry. Toward travellers: a relentless pursuer; once they have your scent they are hard to shake.

lore.en: Orcs trained to hunt by scent and sign, set on the trail of escaped thralls, spies or travellers. Tenacious and savage, the elite among them can follow a cold trail for days and rarely give up a quarry once found.

aspect.en: The tall, fair, long-lived descendants of the Men of Númenor — heirs of a great lost kingdom, noble in bearing and with traces of Elven blood — who founded Arnor and Gondor in exile. Toward travellers: proud, grave and honourable; just and protective toward the free, stern toward the Enemy's servants.

lore.en: The Dúnedain are descendants of the Edain who settled on the island kingdom of Númenor during the Second Age. It was their Númenorean forefathers who colonized and conquered much of Middle-earth. When the Isle of the West sank into the sea during the Downfall of S.A. 3319, two groups survived: the Black Númenoreans and the Faithful Dúnedain. The latter settled Arnor and Gondor, the Realms in Exile. Like all their brethren, they have traces of Elven and Maia blood. Physical Character: Tall and strong. Men average 225 pounds, women 150 pounds. Fair skin and black or dark brown hair. They have grey, hazel, blue, or green eyes. Considerable endurance. Men average 6'5", women 5'10". Lifespan: 100-300 years. Rich and well made, with elaborate collars. The Dúnedain of lowland Gondor wear light tunics and often go without leggings. Those of colder areas wear more. They favor feathers and white symbols on dark fields. Comfortable and centered around cosmopolitan cities and towns. The Dúnedain hate the Corsairs, for they blame them for the Kin-strife, Gondor's civil war. They also despise the Black Númenoreans.

aspect.en: Cold, white, incorporeal figures akin to ghosts and hungry for life-energy — their victims often rise as specters in turn; ordinary weapons cannot touch them. Toward travellers: a draining, fear-wielding haunt of pits and haunted depths that mere steel cannot harm.

lore.en: Uncommon in Middle-earth, Specters are cold, white, incorporeal figures akin to Ghosts. Victims killed by Specters frequently become Specters themselves. The Balrog of Moria, for instance, had his minions throw captives into caverns and pits known to be haunted by these creatures. The Specters' need for energy is so great that even the lesser kind drain 8 points of constitution per round. They cannot be affected by nonmagical weapons because of their insubstantial nature. The Specters of Moria can cast Shock Bolts, in addition to their energydraining abilities.

aspect.en: Tall, gaunt, pale orcs that endure the sun, descended from Morgoth's northern guards and ruling the frozen wastes from a dark ice-fortress; they raid the local peoples, worship Morgoth in grisly festivals, and now serve the Witch-king uneasily. Toward travellers: hostile killers of the far North, hardy in cold and unafraid of daylight.

lore.en: Tall, gaunt, pale, sun-tolerant Orcs descended from Morgoth's northern guards, ruling the Forodwaith from the Dark-Ice Fortress and mining outposts like Thollakar; they raid neighboring Lotan and Lossoth, worship Morgoth in gruesome festivals, and now answer uneasily to the Witch-king of Angmar.[file:38]

aspect.en: Enormous black bears up to 1,400 lbs, marked brown on paws, ears and face, with claws that rend metal and leather — yet shy creatures that prefer roots, berries and fish, and keep close family bonds. Toward travellers: avoid people, but catastrophic if surprised, cornered, or near their cubs.

lore.en: Huge bears (Q. "Meglirondor") weighing up to 1,400 lbs, with rough black fur striped brown on paws, ears and face. Paws can snap a neck and claws rend light metal or leather like linen, yet they are retiring creatures preferring roots, berries and fish. Monogamous and family-minded; males travel alone while females keep their cubs until grown.

aspect.en: Large black crows of evil bent, often servants of dark powers — carrion-eaters that mob the injured, or hunt lone and lost travellers on an evil master's command; keen-eyed and drawn to bright things, they make excellent spies. Toward travellers: an ill sign — their wheeling flocks may be the Enemy's eyes, and they harry the helpless.

lore.en: Large black crows with evil natures, Crebain (sing. "Craban") have often been servants of evil. They are primarily carrion eaters, and they are not picky about how long their meals have been dead or even about whether they are truly dead yet. They will also mob injured creatures and, if under instructions from some evil intelligence, uninjured individuals travelling alone or lost. Keen-sighted and attracted by shining or brightly-colored objects, they make excellent spies. They are most common on south-central Middle-earth, including Fangorn and Dunland, but may be found elsewhere, especially near centers of evil.

aspect.en: Trees grown strange and half-awake — something between tree and Ent — that can move slowly and feel anger, gathering in the deep shadow of Fangorn and the old forests. Toward travellers: those who stray among them when they are roused seldom return.

lore.en: Huorns — trees grown strange and half-awake, between tree and Ent, that can move slowly and feel anger. They gather in the deep shadows of Fangorn and the old forests, and folk who stray among them when they are roused seldom return.

aspect.en: A short, stocky northern folk said to spring from an ancient union of Men and Dwarves — strong, ruddy, red-haired and bearded, supremely hardy in cold but ill-suited to heat, and long-lived. Toward travellers: tough, insular cold-country folk; gruff with strangers but no enemy to honest travellers.

lore.en: The Umli live in the Far North of north-central Middle-earth, east of the Lossoth. They are a race of short folk who apparently came from an ancient union of Men and Dwarves. Legends call them Half-dwarves. Physical Character: Strong and compact, with large features and considerable facial hair. Males average 150 pounds; females 135 pounds. Ruddy skin and red hair, with penetrating pale blue eyes. Exceptional endurance in cold climes; average in temperate areas; poor in warm or hot climates. 4-5 feet. Lifespan: 100-200 years. +30 bonus versus cold/ice attacks and a -15 bonus versus heat/fire attacks. Need sleep but three hours a day. In the cold (below 35°) they halve any encumbrance penalties; above 90° they suffer double encumbrance penalties. Hunters, gatherers, and fisherman, they move from site to site depending on the season. Most reside in caves or underground settlements. Many mine, and the Umli are accomplished smiths and artisans.

aspect.en: A small, easily-overlooked grey snake of western Harad, rarely two feet long, whose wide mouth holds tiny needle-teeth that each inject venom; its poison is so potent that locals reckon amputation the only sure cure for a bite. Toward travellers: deceptively deadly — a drab little snake with one of the most lethal bites.

lore.en: The Otravati (Ap. "Poison"; pl. "Otrovativi") is a small snake found in western Harad. Rarely exceeding two feet in length, it has a murky grey coloring and is easy to overlook. It is, however, not an animal to take lightly. The Otravati's narrow head opens to reveal a surprisingly large mouth full of tiny needle-like teeth. Each tooth is an injector that delivers a dose of the snake's poison on any successful bite (whenever a critical is scored). Locals consider amputation to be the only effective remedy when confronted by the snake's potent (25th lvl) venom, a nerve poison that attacks through the bloodstream and the nervous system simultaneously. The venom is lethal within one hour; only immediate removal of the bitten member will serve as a cure. It is no wonder that the snake bears a name which translates as "poison."

aspect.en: A volcanic kind of fire-drake at home among cinder, ash and lava-fields. Toward travellers: a fire-dragon of the burning wastes, deadly and camouflaged amid the smoke and stone of its lairs.

lore.en: An ash/volcanic variety of Fire-drake, at home amid cinder and lava fields.

aspect.en: Men of the fallen kingdom of Rhudaur, many of whom — land-hungry peasants especially — enlisted in Angmar's armies and later settled as soldier-farmers in fortified villages. Toward travellers: hardened border folk, some still bound to old Angmar loyalties; wary and not always friendly.

lore.en: Men of the former kingdom of Rhudaur; many soldiers, especially land-hungry peasants, enlist in Angmar's armies and later settle as soldier-farmers in fortified villages.

aspect.en: Durin's heirs and people who, after losing Moria, founded scattered mining colonies and later rejoined Erebor — ruled by a king and his lords, with wardens over the outlying holds. Toward travellers: proud, industrious and clannish, guarded with strangers but fair to honest dealers and firm allies.

lore.en: Durin's heirs and their people who, after the loss of Moria, established mining colonies at Silverplunge, Thunderclift, Silverpit, Long Peak and Norr-dum, and later reconnected with Erebor; ruled by a king advised by Dwarf-lords and by appointed Wardens in outlying colonies.[file:38]

aspect.en: Huge, brutish trolls that turn to stone in sunlight, lurking in rocky hills and caves and coming out by night; strong and slow-witted but immensely dangerous. Toward travellers: deadly after dark, killing the unwary — but they can be outlasted until dawn turns them to stone.

lore.en: Trolls that turn to stone when exposed to sunlight, found in rocky areas and hills.

aspect.en: Smaller, marsh-dwelling cousins of the forest boar, prized for hunting and eating — the males dangerous if cornered, slashing with the long tusks they use to root in mud, and fonder than other pigs of berries, insects and fish. Toward travellers: avoids people, but a cornered boar's tusks are a real danger.

lore.en: Smaller than their forest-dwelling relatives that gorge on autumn nuts, Fen Boars make for good hunting and tasty eating. Males can be dangerous if cornered, lashing with the long tusks they normally use to dig mud for roots and grub out rotten meat. More than other pigs they relish berries, insects and fish alongside their usual vegetarian diet.

aspect.en: Large forest and mountain bears, mostly solitary and slow to anger but immensely strong when roused — omnivores that fish, dig and raid for food, a great old one standing taller than a Man and shrugging off all but the heaviest blows. Toward travellers: avoid people, but catastrophic if surprised, cornered, or near cubs.

lore.en: Large forest and mountain bears, mostly solitary and slow to anger but immensely strong when roused. Omnivorous foragers, they fish, dig and raid for food; a great old bear can stand taller than a Man and shrug off all but the heaviest blows.

aspect.en: The rare children of an Elf and a mortal, who at adulthood must choose to live as mortal Men or immortal Elves — strong, slender and gifted with the grace of both kindreds. Toward travellers: uncommon and remarkable, noble and self-possessed, bearing something of both worlds.

lore.en: Half-elves are a rare breed, the offspring of Men and Elves. While the Dúnedain, Corsairs, and Black Númenoreans have Elvish (and even Maia) blood, their connection to Elves lies in the remote past and they are not called Half-elves. True Half-elves have one Elven parent and one Mannish parent. Upon reaching adulthood, a Half-elf must decide whether to live as a mortal Man or an immortal Elf. Elrond of Rivendell chose the latter course, while his brother Elros - first King of Númenor - opted for mortality. Physical Character: Strong and slender, thinner than Men but stouter than Elves. They have thin, angular features. Males average 200 pounds, females 140 pounds. Fair, generally with brown or black hair and grey eyes. Considerable endurance. Half-elves need but 4 hours rest a day: sleep for mortals or meditation for the immortals. Males average 6'3", females 5'11". Mortal Half-elves live 250-500 years. Virtually immune to disease and natural illness. +5 bonus against cold attacks. Can see extremely well in the dark. Under moonlight or starlight they can see perfectly for 500'.

aspect.en: A ruin or relic of Arthedain, the lost northern Dúnedain kingdom — a fallen watchtower, road-marker or hall crumbling on the downs of old Arnor; some still hold lore, treasure or older guardians. Toward travellers: a melancholy landmark and possible shelter, though what lingers in such places is not always friendly.

lore.en: A ruin or relic of Arthedain, northern kingdom of the Dúnedain — a fallen watchtower, road-marker or hall crumbling on the downs of old Arnor. Some still hold lore, treasure or older guardians.

aspect.en: Broken walls, fallen towers and roofless halls left by some vanished people — a haunt of beasts, outlaws and worse, and a lure to treasure-seekers. Toward travellers: shelter and the promise of finds, but most ruins hold more danger than reward for the unprepared.

lore.en: Broken walls, fallen towers and roofless halls left by some vanished people — a haunt of beasts, outlaws and worse, and a lure to treasure-seekers. Most ruins hold more danger than reward for the unprepared.

aspect.en: The noblest of all birds, made by the Valar and as wise as any of the Free Peoples — vast eagles who have borne rescue to great figures in their darkest hours and serve as far-seeing watchers of the world. Toward travellers: aloof and rarely seen, but a friend to the good in dire need; never to be commanded.

lore.en: The Great Eagles are the most noble of all birds, having been created by the Valar Manwe, Lord of the Air, and Yavanna, Queen of the Earth. Appointed as overseers of all the Kelvar, they have played many glorious roles in the history of Middle-earth. They have rescued numerous champions in their hour of greatest need: both the Noldo Elf Maedhros, imprisoned in Thangorodrim, and Gandalf the Grey, confined at Orthanc by Saruman, owe their salvation to these graceful creatures (they also aided Gandalf after his combat with the Balrog of Moria). Great Eagles are as intelligent as any of the Free Peoples but are not numbered among them, presumably because they lack the power to build things and fashion crafts. These huge birds are not to be trifled with: fierce foes when aroused to anger, with little patience for faint-heartedness in the face of danger. They are stalwart foes of Evil and especially hate any other creature of the air who has allied with the Valar enemies.

aspect.en: Black carrion-birds that gather wherever death and battle lie, clever and watchful; flocks of them serve darker powers as spies, and their wheeling overhead is read as an ill omen. Toward travellers: harmless in themselves, but their presence may mean watching eyes.

lore.en: Black carrion-birds that gather wherever death and battle are found, clever and watchful. Flocks of them serve as the eyes of darker powers, and their wheeling overhead is an ill omen to wary travellers.

aspect.en: A small swamp turtle of Fangorn, its shell about a foot and a half across, with a long neck it can strike out like a snake to deliver a paralysing venom. Toward travellers: harmless unless handled or stepped on, when its quick, numbing bite is a nasty surprise.

lore.en: Blue Terrapins (Q. "Luinikrúmori"; sing. "Luinikrúmor") are only found in thickets or very dense, overgrown swamp areas. Their native home is Fangorn Forest. Small, their shells average 18" across, but they have a 12" neck. Thus, a Blue Terrapin can strike like a snake, delivering a 2nd level muscle poison (with a Critical Strike) that can paralyze a small mammal (up to 40 lbs). If it bites, it will paralyze the area or limb it penetrates, partially paralyzing one adjacent area. The poison wears off in 3 hours.

aspect.en: Huge, intelligent enchanted wolves first made by Morgoth — able to stand and use clawed hands, to speak, use tools and cast spells, though never to become Men. Toward travellers: a cunning, sorcerous predator far worse than any natural wolf, hunting the dark woods.

lore.en: Huge, intelligent enchanted wolves first made by Morgoth, able to stand and use clawlike hands, speak, use tools and cast spells but never become Men. Caran-Carach (Red Fang) guarded Dol Guldur, home of the Necromancer, and hunted the Wood-elves and Wood-men of southern Mirkwood.

aspect.en: Sauron's orcs infesting the ancient Dwarf-halls of Moria, plundering its vaults and dens. Toward travellers: hostile and deadly in the dark; they swarm and hunt any who enter the old mines.

lore.en: Sauron's servants who plunder the ancient dwarven vaults.

aspect.en: Tall, long-legged domestic dogs of Dúnedain lands, with short wiry russet coats — sure-footed, strong swimmers, keen-nosed, fearless and loyal, favoured by shepherds, herders and hunters. Toward travellers: loyal working dogs, friendly with their folk but staunch guardians against intruders.

lore.en: Tall, domesticated dogs found wherever the Dunedain have resided or held extensive commercial links, with long legs and short wiry coats of dark brown or russet. Well-liked by shepherds, herders and hunters, they are sure-footed, good swimmers, keen-nosed, fearless and loyal, and are often fitted with collars and even leather coats.

aspect.en: Hardy wild and half-wild goats browsing rough hills, crags and scrub where better pasture fails — sure-footed and tough, kept by hill-folk for milk, hair and meat. Toward travellers: harmless; a sign of high, rough country and the folk who work it.

lore.en: Hardy goats, wild and half-wild, browsing the rough hills, crags and scrub where richer pasture fails. Sure-footed and tough, kept by hill-folk for milk, hair and meat and run wild across the uplands.

aspect.en: A tiny, vivid lime-green tree-frog of the far-southern rainforest, streaked yellow and orange, exuding a potent contact poison from its skin; rare and hard to find despite its bright warning colours. Toward travellers: deadly to touch — hunters take it only with nets, never bare hands.

lore.en: A small tree frog from the rainforests of the Mûmakan in the south of Middle-earth, the Umak (pl. "Umakavi") is notable for the potent contact poison exuded by its colorful skin. Bright lime green and streaked with yellow and orange, the Umak Tree Frog is noticeable, but it is so rare that it is still nearly impossible to spot. The bright coloring warns away animal and bird predators who would be poisoned upon grabbing the frog in their beaks or mouths, but merely makes things easier for clever human or Elf hunters who come armed with nets on long handles. The poison is tenth level in contact with skin; unlucky individuals are killed instantly (upon failing a RR), while the more fortunate are plunged into a coma until awakened by some form of antidote.

aspect.en: A heat-sensing venomous snake of warm rock and scrub that strikes from ambush with a swift, deadly bite — well camouflaged and slow to flee, endangering any who clamber carelessly among its stones. Toward travellers: a hidden, deadly bite for the careless climber; watch hand and foot among warm rocks.

lore.en: A heat-sensing venomous snake of warm rock and scrub, striking from ambush with a swift, deadly bite. Well camouflaged and slow to flee, it endangers any who clamber carelessly among its stones.

aspect.en: An evergreen coastal tree of Tolfalas and Gondor's seaward fringe, glossy-leaved and aromatic with resin, weathering salt winds and binding cliffs and dunes with its roots. Toward travellers: harmless; a hardy mark of the windswept coast.

lore.en: The Oiolair is an evergreen coastal tree associated with the isle of Tolfalas and the seaward fringes of Gondor. With glossy leaves and aromatic resin, it weathers salt winds and storms, binding cliffs and dunes with its roots.

aspect.en: Large, intelligent cousins of the timber wolf across the North, deeply social and mated for life, hunting in cooperative packs; unlike common wolves they little fear the Free Peoples and will hunt Men, Elves or Dwarves. Toward travellers: a bold, clever and dangerous pack-hunter unafraid of people, a real threat especially in numbers.

lore.en: Large cousin (S. "Gothraug") of the Timber Wolf, found all over northern Middle-earth in family groups (2-11) or packs (10-60). Intelligent, social and mated for life, settling disputes without bloodshed and cooperating in the hunt; unlike common wolves they have little fear of the Free Peoples and will hunt Men, Elves or Dwarves. Up to 150 lbs, 30 mph, leaping 6 ft, with tremendous nightvision.

aspect.en: Dust first. (authored encounter `GZ-01`)

lore.en: Dust first. Then the noise, of wheels and animals, unlike anything else in the region. If he asks to travel with them, the master will look him up and down and decide in ten seconds.

aspect.en: Six or eight riders on small horses, appearing off a hill and circling him unhurried. (authored encounter `GZ-02`)

lore.en: Six or eight riders on small horses, appearing off a hill and circling him unhurried. They draw nothing. One comes forward and talks, and speaks the common tongue enough.

aspect.en: A badly made camp in a copse: no pen, no order, rubbish about. (authored encounter `GZ-06`)

lore.en: A badly made camp in a copse: no pen, no order, rubbish about. There are five or six, badly armed and worse fed. And the first thing he notices is that they do not speak the same tongue among themselves, and that the one in charge is not fully in charge.

aspect.en: A well-made cart, painted, with awning, drawn by two good animals, two people up front talking. (authored encounter `GZ-08`)

lore.en: A well-made cart, painted, with awning, drawn by two good animals, two people up front talking. They carry incredible things: dwarven tools, bells, mechanical toys, dyed cloth. And they go alone, on the road, with that on board, southeastward.

aspect.en: They are the first he has seen in days and they speak his own language, well, without a forest accent. (authored encounter `DG-06`)

lore.en: They are the first he has seen in days and they speak his own language, well, without a forest accent. They ask about the road behind: whether it is passable, whether he saw anyone, how many people are at the burned clearing this week. Reasonable questions from people who travel.

aspect.en: Ash still warm at the bottom edge. (authored encounter `DG-10`)

lore.en: Ash still warm at the bottom edge. A flattened place in the leaf-litter where somebody slept. A stake driven in with a strip of cloth tied to it, the kind used to hang things so they do not get eaten.

aspect.en: He sits down beside him without asking leave and begins with a question about the outside: how the road is, what there is to see in the north, whether it is true that Esgaroth has a market all year. (authored encounter `WM-04`)

lore.en: He sits down beside him without asking leave and begins with a question about the outside: how the road is, what there is to see in the north, whether it is true that Esgaroth has a market all year. He listens to the answer hungrily. Then he talks.

aspect.en: He is walking and there is somebody ahead, twenty paces off, still, watching him. (authored encounter `WR-06`)

lore.en: He is walking and there is somebody ahead, twenty paces off, still, watching him. It speaks to him in his own language, well, and asks two questions. The tone is not an interrogation's: it is that of somebody who needs the datum.

aspect.en: A circle of wagons, eighty or a hundred, shafts inward and wheels chocked, forming a closed yard. (authored encounter `ET-05`)

lore.en: A circle of wagons, eighty or a hundred, shafts inward and wheels chocked, forming a closed yard. Inside, the livestock. And around the circle, outside, the felt tents and the fires.

aspect.en: Dust first, for hours. (authored encounter `DR-03`)

lore.en: Dust first, for hours. Then, a column: wagons, riders, livestock, people on foot, moving in order, miles long. They cross the steppe fast, water calculated to the last skin, and do not stop except where stopping is needed.

aspect.en: Dwarves with a different accent. (authored encounter `EH-06`)

lore.en: Dwarves with a different accent. If he has been in the Blue Mountains he will notice at once: they speak the common tongue with another music, and use words not used there. And they are young.

aspect.en: Small camps, four or five hide tents, in the high valleys. (authored encounter `EH-07`)

lore.en: Small camps, four or five hide tents, in the high valleys. Goat herds, the only thing this land feeds. And lean hard people, hide-clad, with short bows.

aspect.en: He is camped or walking at night, and there is light between the trees. (authored encounter `WR-05`)

lore.en: He is camped or walking at night, and there is light between the trees. This time there is a smell of food and voices singing, and the voices are clearly voices and clearly singing well. If he has already seen `MW-03`, the first thing he will think is that they are the other lights.

aspect.en: Somebody sitting at a longhouse door, doing something with their hands. (authored encounter `RH-09`)

lore.en: Somebody sitting at a longhouse door, doing something with their hands. If the traveller asks about a name, a family or a place, they will straighten up and begin. And they will not stop.

aspect.en: He may run into the party going out, at night, quiet, dogs on leash. (authored encounter `RH-10`)

lore.en: He may run into the party going out, at night, quiet, dogs on leash. Or he may be in the village when the recovery party returns, by day, with the cattle and in very good humour. If he is in a village when the others arrive, nobody will involve him.

aspect.en: Two men beside a small fire, in a spot he would not have chosen and that turns out better than the one he chose. (authored encounter `RH-14`)

lore.en: Two men beside a small fire, in a spot he would not have chosen and that turns out better than the one he chose. They share what they have. They ask little and listen very carefully.

aspect.en: Six or seven head grazing in a valley, two days from the nearest village, nobody around. (authored encounter `RH-16`)

lore.en: Six or seven head grazing in a valley, two days from the nearest village, nobody around. Butchering one is very easy. It is the easiest food in the region.

aspect.en: Almost always, nothing. (authored encounter `FG-07`)

lore.en: Almost always, nothing. He walks among trees. But at some point, in a particular stand, he will notice that things changed.

aspect.en: They will ask him to let them blindfold him. (authored encounter `LO-02`)

lore.en: They will ask him to let them blindfold him. They will ask courteously and they will not argue it. If he refuses, the matter is over and he goes back the way he came.

aspect.en: He notices them because they are following him badly. (authored encounter `SH-07`)

lore.en: He notices them because they are following him badly. Very badly. At fifty paces, hiding behind hedges that do not cover them, talking to each other in perfectly audible whispers.

aspect.en: He sees the glow before the fire, orange between the trunks, and his first thought is a camp. (authored encounter `TS-11`)

lore.en: He sees the glow before the fire, orange between the trunks, and his first thought is a camp. His second, that there are no night camps here. He comes close enough to hear and then he understands, and what convinces him is not the size of the silhouettes: it is the volume.

aspect.en: One or two in the corner of the room, good-quality worn clothes, quiet, eating slowly. (authored encounter `BR-10`)

lore.en: One or two in the corner of the room, good-quality worn clothes, quiet, eating slowly. They do not seek conversation. If the traveller approaches well, they answer precisely and in few words.

aspect.en: He finds him bent over, cutting, and the elf does not raise his head until the traveller is beside him. (authored encounter `LI-O1`)

lore.en: He finds him bent over, cutting, and the elf does not raise his head until the traveller is beside him. He answers everything asked and answers well, with exact information on roads, fords, distances and weather. And in the same reply, in the same tone and without lowering his voice, he will tell him something that cannot be true.

aspect.en: He sees it among the trunks, standing, watching him, forty paces off. (authored encounter `LI-O3`)

lore.en: He sees it among the trunks, standing, watching him, forty paces off. When the traveller takes a step, the deer takes a step. When he stops, it stops.

aspect.en: If the day falls right, the whole town is at the bay and there are people who came from three days away. (authored encounter `LI-T7`)

lore.en: If the day falls right, the whole town is at the bay and there are people who came from three days away. The technical part takes the morning: wedges, grease on the ways, hawsers, and thirty people hauling a rope at once while somebody marks the rhythm with their voice. The hull enters the water and floats, and there is a short silence before somebody applauds.

aspect.en: Two or three men in a corner of the room, sitting with their backs to the wall. (authored encounter `SA-03`)

lore.en: Two or three men in a corner of the room, sitting with their backs to the wall. Tall, dark-haired, grey or brown cloaks without blazon, worn boots, gear in order. They are quiet and they are listening.

aspect.en: There is somebody sitting by the fire when he arrives, or somebody arrives when he is already there. (authored encounter `GL-01`)

lore.en: There is somebody sitting by the fire when he arrives, or somebody arrives when he is already there. They share whatever they have without discussing it. They talk of what is around: the state of the road, a tree, the rain, a bird that passed.

aspect.en: He sees them coming head-on, in file, at a steady pace. (authored encounter `AM-03`)

lore.en: He sees them coming head-on, in file, at a steady pace. They do not hide and do not hurry. The corporal raises a hand and the column stops. He speaks to him in Westron, badly. The questions are short. Who, from where, to where. Then they search. They make him drop everything on the road and open it there, on the ground, the wind taking whatever weighs nothing. They take much longer than needed. One of the six takes his coat to look it over front and back. When done he does not hand it back at once: he keeps it over his arm a while, looking at something else, while the traveller stands in the north wind in his shirtsleeves. The corporal sees it and says nothing. Then they give some things back.

aspect.en: It is already night when it starts. (authored encounter `TM-26`)

lore.en: It is already night when it starts. One long howl, alone, that rises and breaks off. Then, from another side, another answers. Then a third, and it is no longer possible to tell how many there are. The traveller stops what he was doing and listens. He tries to judge the distance and cannot. Suddenly they all fall silent at once, and that silence is worse than the noise.

aspect.en: The first thing he notices is more tracks and fewer animals. (authored encounter `TM-21`)

lore.en: The first thing he notices is more tracks and fewer animals. The second is that here they come closer sooner. Not in full night: at dusk, in light still. The third is that if he has a fire, they stay thirty paces off, sitting, and do not leave all night.

aspect.en: A wolf trail in the snow: fifteen or twenty animals in single file, each stepping in the print before, which is what wolves do and why they cannot be counted well. (authored encounter `TM-09`)

lore.en: A wolf trail in the snow: fifteen or twenty animals in single file, each stepping in the print before, which is what wolves do and why they cannot be counted well. It crosses his course and he follows it a while because it is easy walking.

aspect.en: If he meets one alone, the bear will look at him and most likely leave. (authored encounter `TM-06`)

lore.en: If he meets one alone, the bear will look at him and most likely leave. What must not be done is standing between a bear and its food, or near the cubs.

aspect.en: He smells them before he sees them: the smell of the camp smoke, but raw, greener, without the sweetness of the berries. (authored encounter `TM-27`)

lore.en: He smells them before he sees them: the smell of the camp smoke, but raw, greener, without the sweetness of the berries. Three women are crouched on the slope, pulling up clumps of a low grey herb and putting them in leather bags. Every clump they pull releases that smell. They see him, nod to him and keep working. If he comes close, one of them puts a leaf in his hand, presses it between his fingers so it releases the smell, and tells him that this is what keeps you from sleeping.

aspect.en: A man alone, on foot, in mid-afternoon, with a horn hung from his shoulder that trails a thread of smoke. (authored encounter `TM-28`)

lore.en: A man alone, on foot, in mid-afternoon, with a horn hung from his shoulder that trails a thread of smoke. The smoke smells like the camps'. He does not hide and does not hurry. When they meet, he raises the horn by way of greeting. He is heading for the nearest copse. If the traveller goes with him, he sees him uncover the horn, blow the embers onto a handful of bark and throw the mix on top. With the fire lit, the man stacks the woodpile and goes on to the next copse.
The last hobbit of an emptied marsh, saving for the Shire.

notes.en: A hundred years old, the last hobbit of a marsh emptied by the Plague — fish, a pipe-weed patch he guards like treasure, traps on every path, and carrier-pigeons to the few cousins left. He will guide you to the strange mirror in the reeds for a hundred mo, not to cheat you: he needs the tavern-money and there are no hobbit-women here.

aspect.en: Small neat snares along the marsh-paths, smoke from a hidden chimney, and a pigeon with a message-tube going east.

text.en: A tree-house in the drowned woods where a hobbit-village used to stand — snares on every path, a little patch of pipe-weed hoed to perfection, and a fat, bristling old hobbit who greets you through a window with a fishing-rod. For a hundred mo he will take you to the strange mirror in the reeds. He is not cheating; he is fundraising.

lore.en: Old Maggot's temper in a Bree-land orchard.

notes.en:
A hobbit with a spread of apple-trees outside Bree and three large dogs with opinions — he sells cider at the Pony, mistrusts everyone
    north of his gate on principle, and has been watching the strange
    times with a loaded cart and a loaded worry.

aspect.en: Apple-rows running to the hedge, three large dog-shapes holding a line, and a hobbit on the cart watching the road like weather.

text.en: A hobbit-farmer works the apple-rows with three serious dogs holding a perimeter — Grip, Fang, and the big one that doesn't need a name. If your business is apples or cider he is excellent company; if it is any kind of funny business the dogs settle it. He has opinions about the dark riders that are worth a pint to hear.

lore.en: A ranger who looks like trouble to people who have not met him.

notes.en: The long hunt is done: he took the creature in the Dead Marshes and now walks it north, nine hundred miles of rope and patience, to Thranduil's keeping. Afterwards — the wild again, watching the roads no one else watches.

aspect.en: A tall ranger passed leading something that was not a prisoner and not a man, on the end of a rope; they travelled by night where they could.

text.en: A hard-faced man in weathered green goes north with a hooded thing on a rope — it whimpers and curses softly to itself. He warns you off with a look rather than a word: this is errantry you do not want to be curious about.

aspect.en: A ranger's pipe-smoke in the ruins at dusk; travellers say the watch on the northern roads is not wholly gone.

text.en: A tall weather-beaten man who answers, eventually, to Strider. He knows things about the roads that innkeepers don't, shares a fire and little else, and is gone before first light.

lore.en: A bear of a man who expects the end and keeps the larder full anyway.

notes.en: Seventy winters and still the strongest thing in the Vales. He keeps a hidden cabin packed with meat and cheese against the day — he is sure it is coming — when the Dark Lord takes everything. He resists. He does not trust you yet.

aspect.en: A bear's track that ends in a man's boot-print, and a wood-path that is watched — the trail is honest but the ambush is not.

variants.title: The old bear of the Vales

text.en: A grey-bearded old man, broad as a door, standing between you and a wood-path that clearly goes somewhere he doesn't show. The Vales folk say he is kind to the starving and terrible to the armed — and that some nights what walks his woods is a bear the size of a hay-cart. He is listening to your voice for the lie in it.

lore.en: A squint-eyed man of Bree whose curiosity is for sale.

notes.en: Eyes and ears on the Bree gate for a southern paymaster he does not name — every stranger noted, every unusual name repeated north. When the raid comes he will already be gone.

text.en: A squint-eyed man lounges where he can see who comes and goes, and remembers names the way a merchant remembers debts. He asks after queer names — elvish names, hobbit names — with a friendliness that does not reach his eyes.

lore.en: Two old men in sea-blue, at work where the maps end.

notes.en: Alatar and Pallando — the two who went east and did not come back. What they do out there is not written in any western book: some say they stir up resistance against the Dark Lord, some say they shelter the peoples the world forgot. Both are probably true.

aspect.en: The wain-folk speak, not loudly, of two old men in sea-blue who walk the east as if it were a garden they are weeding.

text.en: Two old men in sea-blue robes walk the wain-roads like they own the weather. One is kind-eyed and says nothing; the other watches everything. Where they pass, the talk in the caravans quiets — not from fear, from a strange instinct that two very old arguments are being carried on by these two, and have been for centuries.

lore.en: Eldest; a song that has been in the forest longer than the forest.

notes.en: Bright blue his jacket is and his boots are yellow — and he is master of wood, water and hill, singing to it as it was and as it is, quite indifferent to the Ring and everything the Ring will change.

aspect.en: Singing in the Old Forest — nonsense-words and river-names, a voice too happy to be safe and too merry to fear.

text.en: A stout fellow in blue jacket and yellow boots, gathering water lilies and singing to them as if they were guests. The old trees lean away from him respectfully. He asks your name the way the sky asks nothing; he has been here longer than the asking of questions.

lore.en: The Captain of the White Tower, riding alone into lands his maps call wild.

notes.en: Seek for the sword that was broken: a dream sent twice to his brother and once to him, and no clearer answer in Gondor than a name — Imladris. A hundred and ten days on the road for a riddle.

aspect.en: A tall soldier of the South passed asking the way to Imladris — proud-spoken, road-worn, travelling alone.

variants.title: The Captain of the White Tower

text.en: A big man on a tired horse, armed like a war-captain and dusty like a beggar — the horn at his side is worth more than everything else he owns. He asks about a valley called Imladris as if he expects the name to hurt him. He has come a very long way for a dream.

lore.en: Master of the Prancing Pony; a good man with a bad memory and a worse autumn ahead.

notes.en: Keep the Pony full and the guests fed — and worry, increasingly, about the sort of folk the roads have started delivering to his door.

text.en: Butterbur is everywhere at once in the big inn — tankards in both hands, two conversations at once, apologising to a third. Business is bad, he says, the roads are full of queer folk, and something in the way he says it suggests he would rather you asked no questions and took a room for the night.

lore.en: The spectres that answer theft in the field of the dead.

notes.en: The dead of the battle-plain do not sleep, and they remember being burgled. Whatever is taken from Dagorlad is hunted across Dagorlad — and the marsh is very good at keeping what it is given.

aspect.en: Lights like candle-flames stand above the pools at night — the old dead marshalling again, and where they pass the mists go cold as a crypt.

text.en: Pale lights marshal over the black water, and the mist itself arranges into ranks — the armies of the plain rising one more time to collect what is owed. Nothing living is meant to see this. Nothing that sees it stays entirely living.

lore.en: Brog does not fish and Liss does not fight — two wretched immortals arguing in a speech that is almost Westron and mostly splashing, condemned to each other in a swamp that does not forget.

notes.en: Two of four bandits who hid in the marsh of the dead and robbed the jewels from ancient corpses — and the jewels keep them alive. Two who tried to walk out with the loot were chased down by the spectres; these two learned. Near a hundred years together now, looking barely fifty, hating each other with the patience of the undying — the big one cannot fish, the small one cannot fight.

aspect.en: Two voices quarrel in the mists — almost Westron, mostly splashing — and a fire too small for honest travellers smokes among the pools.

text.en: They squat by a black pool over a meal of raw fish eaten with their fingers, and they do not stop bickering even as they size you up. Brog is enormous — bald, stone-strong, white beard to the waist — and Liss is a small thin man with a glass eye that does not move. They speak a slurred, deformed Westron you can only half-follow: they are deciding whether your gear is worth the trouble, and the trouble is that nothing is allowed to leave the marsh. Not corpses' jewels, not them — and maybe, they are working out, not you.

lore.en: Not a company but a tide — thousands of orcs under the banner of the Necromancer's tower, marching by night because they can.

notes.en: The army that waits under the dead pines of the south moves at last: north through Mirkwood to burn the Woodland Realm on the same night Osgiliath falls — a war begun everywhere at once, and a door left open for a small thing to escape.

aspect.en: The pines to the east are burning. There is a sound under the smoke like a forge the size of a valley, and the Woodmen have abandoned their villages without a word.

variants.title: The forest itself is an army

text.en: For a day and a night the trees to the east move. Not walking — marching. Fires go up in ranks, like encampments that learned to crawl, and the smoke lies flat across the woods as if the earth is holding its breath. Whatever is inside that smoke has a direction, and the direction is the Woodland Realm, and nothing that still lives between here and there will live long. When it passes, the forest it leaves behind is not merely burned — it is *occupied*: the stumps stand in rows like drilled soldiers, and things with too many eyes have been left behind in the roots to watch.

aspect.en: Orc-sign fresh at dawn: a watch-post pulled down, tracks that double back, and a dead bird nailed to a waymark.

text.en: The army has gone back south to its pits, but it left pieces of itself in the woods — a war-band that did not get the order, or did not want it. They strip the dead, they mark the trees with the eye of the southern tower, and they have not stopped being hungry.

lore.en: Loneliness dressed in old Dúnedain grey, reading the clouds over dead kings.

notes.en: A solitary woman of the dwindled northern people who walks the ruins of Arnor looking at the sky — watching for something she half-believes will come back, in an age when her people have almost stopped believing.

aspect.en: A woman in grey standing alone on a ruin-wall, looking up — the hillfolk say she has been watching the same sky for a year.

text.en: A grey-wrapped woman of the old northern blood stands on a broken wall and watches the western sky the way sailors watch horizons — for sails. She gives her name as Artheniel and little else. Whatever she hopes for out of the west, it has not come yet. She accepts a traveller's company with grave courtesy, talks little, and always ends up looking up.

lore.en: An elf walking west alone, a little behind the singing.

notes.en: She is sailing. He would not. That is the whole story, and she has carried it four hundred miles — with his medallion, the one she had made for him, around her own neck now, because someone has to remember what they looked like.

aspect.en: An elf-woman passed west, walking a little behind the others, turning a small gold thing in her fingers as she went.

text.en: She walks at the back of the company, and while they sing the grey shores she looks at the hills behind. Around her neck, on a chain too fine for the road, a small medallion — made for a man who would not come. If you ask her where she is going she says 'the Sea'. If you ask her what she is leaving, she does not answer.

lore.en: A messenger whose horse is black and whose terms are worse.

notes.en: Out of Mordor to the Lonely Mountain, with the Lord's own courtesy: an alliance for Dáin Ironfoot, friendship for the dwarves — and a small price, a trifle, a little ring that a hobbit-thief once carried.

aspect.en: A lone rider in dark mail went north through the wild lands; the horses he does not buy, he takes.

text.en: A rider who travels by preference at dusk and asks his questions through inn doors rather than inside them. He is bound for the Mountain and speaks of friendship between great powers — but the horse is black, the mail is black, and the men who let him pass count themselves lucky afterwards.

aspect.en: The dark rider waits under the Mountain still; Dáin has sent no answer and opens no door.

text.en: At the gate of the Kingdom under the Mountain a messenger waits for a reply that will not come, patient as grave-dirt. The dwarves will not say what was asked, only that the asking must never be repeated.

lore.en: The Lossoth name it Tursas — the least of the old fire's children, but still more than enough.

notes.en: Not one of the great worms of the ancient world — a cold-drake of the northern wastes, fireless but not toothless, roaming the frozen moors for reindeer and the occasional unlucky man, and denned through the deep winter in a cave that smells like the inside of a forge.

aspect.en: A reek of sulphur hangs over the moor though there is no forge for a hundred miles, and the reindeer are running from nothing.

text.en: You smell it before you see it — sulphur and wet stone, like the inside of a smithy buried under a mountain. Then the moor blinks. A cold-drake, wingless and grey as old ice, watching you with the patience of a thing that does not hurry its food. It is not Smaug. It is only what is left of dragons — which is enough.

aspect.en: Travellers know the cave by the smell — sulphur deep in the rock — and by the bones kicked out onto the ice.

text.en: The cave mouth breathes warm, sulphurous air into the frozen dark. Inside, something mountain-sized turns over in its sleep and the stone groans. Whatever you needed shelter from, this is worse.

aspect.en: A reek of sulphur hangs over the moor though there is no forge for a hundred miles, and the reindeer are running from nothing.

text.en: You smell it before you see it — sulphur and wet stone, like the inside of a smithy buried under a mountain. Then the moor blinks. A cold-drake, wingless and grey as old ice, watching you with the patience of a thing that does not hurry its food.

aspect.en: Travellers know the cave by the smell — sulphur deep in the rock — and by the bones kicked out onto the ice.

text.en: The cave mouth breathes warm, sulphurous air into the frozen dark. Inside, something mountain-sized turns over in its sleep and the stone groans. Whatever you needed shelter from, this is worse.

lore.en: The Grey Wanderer; when he moves, something in the world moves with him.

notes.en: Proves beyond doubt that Bilbo's ring is the One: he rides south to read Isildur's scroll in the archives of Minas Tirith, returns to warn Frodo — and is betrayed seeking Saruman's counsel.

aspect.en: A grey rider on a good horse passed east not many days ago, asking after the old roads.

text.en: A grey-cloaked wanderer spurs past without stopping — broad hat bent against the wind, staff laid across the saddle. He has the look of a man with far to go and little time.
A grey old man has been shut in the archive halls for long weeks, the guards say — reading scrolls older than the city.
Gandalf is a guest at Bag End, and the Ivy Bush is full of it — he walks the lanes at dusk, talks long with Frodo behind closed shutters, and looks ten years older than he did.

aspect.en: The grey wanderer rode south at speed; a brown-cloaked oddity was seen asking for him on the same road.

text.en: Gandalf passes south with his hat pulled low. He answers greetings but does not take his eyes off the road, and he does not say where he is going — which, from him, is itself an answer.

aspect.en: A great eagle was seen flying west; and a beggar-man in grey asked for a horse at the king's hall.

text.en: A travel-worn grey figure walks the plain — staff in hand, hat gone, moving with the speed of urgency rather than age. The mark Rohan left on him is not kindness.

aspect.en: A grey horse without equal was seen running the north road, faster than horses run.

text.en: If you passed near the ruin of Amon Sûl in these nights you saw what the shepherds saw: a fire on the hilltop that leapt like lightning, and thunder with no rain — and afterwards, silence, and hoofprints going north faster than any rider should need to go.

aspect.en: Shepherds speak of a tired grey rider slipping north through the wild in the dark hours only.

text.en: A grey figure rides the waste by night, leading shadows away from a road he is not on. He is bait, and he knows it, and he is very good at it.

variants.title: A grey man by Elrond's fire

text.en: A grey old man sits late by the fire in the Last Homely House, smoking in silence. The servants say he asks every guest the same question — whether the hobbit has come yet.

lore.en: High Elves wandering the Shire-woods by starlight, for the last of many autumns.

notes.en: Noldor of the house of Finrod walking the woods they have always loved before the Sea takes them — singing old songs under new stars, and this year, watching the east more carefully than they let on.

aspect.en: Lantern-light and singing in the woods of the east borders — elvish, high and sad, gone by morning.

text.en: Lights in the wood that are not lanterns and a song that is not men's — and for a moment the dark is not dark. They know of the Black Riders, of the east wind, of more than they sing about; if they choose to share it, it will be in their own time and in verse.

lore.en: An extravagant walker whose eyes literally have weather.

notes.en: A wandering eccentric who carries a small case of glass eyes and changes them to match his mood — red-shot for fury, merry green for good days, a sleepily drooping amber for the drowsy miles. Whether it is affectation or something truer, nobody has asked him twice.

aspect.en: A traveller was seen on the south roads with one eye of glass — the colour, witnesses insist, changes with his temper.

text.en: A flamboyant stranger who introduces himself as Amory Bellifont, greets you like a theatre and talks with one eye too still — until mid-conversation he swaps it, from a small velvet case, for one of a friendlier colour. 'For the road,' he explains, offended you'd stare. It is impossible to tell whether you have met a showman, a madman, or a courtesy you haven't earned yet.

lore.en: Two dwarves of Erebor, father and son, armed for a long road and a longer story.

notes.en: Dáin sends them west with two purposes: warn Elrond of the messenger who came to Erebor asking after hobbits and a ring — and carry the memory of an older road to the one house that remembers everything.

aspect.en: Two dwarves of the Mountain were seen on the old forest road — a grey-beard and a young one — singing dwarf-songs under their breath.

text.en: Two dwarves, one grey and one young, mail under travel-cloaks and axes they do not bother to hide. The old one talks of the King under the Mountain and of a shadow-messenger who came to their gate asking after hobbits; the young one watches the road and says little.

lore.en: Not quite a person anymore; not quite anything else either.

notes.en: The thing in the dark remembers only two words: Baggins, and Precious. Caught, caged, escaped — and now loose again in the world, swimming west toward a name he does not understand but cannot let go.

aspect.en: Fisher-folk on the marsh-edge lock their boats at night now; something thin has been seen slipping between the pools.

text.en: Eyes like lamps between the reeds, gone when you look again, and a voice — too thin, too hungry — talking to itself about a precious thing that was stolen.

aspect.en: A woodman's camp raided in the night — only fish taken, only the small tracks left.

text.en: In the confusion of the orc-fires something small went over the wall and into the dark — and if you hear it, you will think it is only the wind crying until it cries a word.

aspect.en: A voice like a wet stone was heard cursing the sun near the eastern walls, and pale marks on the water's edge that are almost hands.

text.en: Something haunts the doors and the dim lake, pressing flat when torches pass — it cannot go in and it will not go away, and it whispers one name over and over to the dark water.

lore.en: The dwarves call it Gormr — a dragon the way a knife is a sword: smaller, still fatal.

notes.en: Young as dragons reckon it, hungry as dwarves reckon it. It denizens the mined-out eastern galleries of the Iron Hills, stealing goats and growing braver — and the dwarves of the Hills have a bounty on it that nobody dares collect.

aspect.en: Goatherds of the Hills count their animals twice since spring, and the count keeps disagreeing; the rafters of an old mine-gallery stink of sulphur.

text.en: Something smaller than legend and bigger than a house slides between the spoil-heaps, trailing a stink of sulphur and bad meat. A young drake — clever enough to hunt close to dwarf-roads because dwarves are rich and goats are not. It has not decided yet whether you are the second kind.

aspect.en: The dwarves mark certain galleries on their maps with a red scratch and the word "his".

variants.title: The gallery that is spoken for

text.en: Deep in a worked-out gallery the air is furnace-warm and the coins and bones underfoot crunch the same way. Young dragons collect things they don't understand, like children — coins, helmets, a goat-bell. And there, atop the small hoard, breathing: the collector.

aspect.en: Goatherds of the Hills count their animals twice since spring, and the count keeps disagreeing; the rafters of an old mine-gallery stink of sulphur.

text.en: Something smaller than legend and bigger than a house slides between the spoil-heaps, trailing a stink of sulphur and bad meat. A young drake — clever enough to hunt close to dwarf-roads because dwarves are rich and goats are not. It has not decided yet whether you are the second kind.

lore.en: The happy kind of ending.

notes.en: Not every road to the Havens is sad: these go singing, young and old together, as if the grey sea were a wedding and not a goodbye. For them the leaving is the easiest thing they have ever done.

aspect.en: Elven singing on the westward road — high, glad, and already half-turned toward the sea.

text.en: A company of elves in travel-green, singing in three voices about white shores. They share their bread without being asked, laugh at your hurry, and wave as if they will see you again — which, in the way of elves going to the Sea, they never quite say.

aspect.en: Elven singing on the westward road — high, glad, and already half-turned toward the sea.

text.en: Another company on the same green road, summer flowers in their hair as if it were a festival. The Sea is taking the elves the way autumn takes the leaves — gladly, in singing, one band at a time.

lore.en: Greybark, who mourns his rowans.

notes.en: One of the three eldest Ents, who loved the mountain-ash above all growing things — and the orcs of the mountains cut his rowan-groves for firewood. He walks the westward slopes now, and his sorrow is a slow storm.

aspect.en: In the high wood, the sound of a voice mourning in a tongue like wind through broken branches — over a hillside of stumps.

text.en: A grey old ent stands over a hillside of stumps — orc-work, years old now — and keens in a slow language that hurts to hear. He does not notice you, or chooses not to. Grief this old does not need witnesses.

lore.en: An elf-lord's son travelling under a burden of bad tidings.

notes.en: Carrying the worst news a messenger can carry: the prisoner is gone. West across Mirkwood and the mountains to Imladris, to tell Elrond that Gollum has escaped — and to arrive, as it happens, in time for a council that will decide everything.

aspect.en: An elf of the woodland passed west — the woodmen say he sang less than elves usually do.

text.en: A tall elf with a long knife and a graver face than elves usually show strangers, travelling fast and light. He is courteous but does not linger; whatever he carries, it weighs more than his pack.

lore.en: A refugee people who wear their survival on their faces — "the Masked", the Easterlings call them; among themselves, the Zimrathân.

notes.en: Descendants of the ones the Blue Wizards slipped out of the Downfall — hidden among the wain-folk for two thousand years, smiths of the living masks, hunting the scattered Númenórean mirrors and dreaming of a Númenor that does not want them back. They are not Sauron's; they are nobody's.

aspect.en: Among the wain-folk's caravan you notice faces that are too still — masks like a second skin, watching for old things with eyes.

text.en: Halfway down the wain-caravan, three travellers whose faces are perfect and dead — masks like a second skin, master-work that even the Easterlings revere. They trade fine steel and ask quiet, careful questions: about ruins, about old Númenórean things, about mirrors that are not mirrors. Their courtesy is real and so is the danger of knowing too much about them.

lore.en: The garrison-army of the corpse-city — soldiers of Mordor with orders written in the Dark Tower itself.

notes.en: Out of Minas Morgul the first open stroke of the war: cross the river, take the east bank of Osgiliath, and hold it while the real hunting goes on elsewhere.

aspect.en: A greenish light stands over the vale of Morgul after dark, and the river-men say the bridge-wardens have doubled their watch.

text.en: In the small hours the Morgul Vale vomits an army — drums that echo wrong off the dead walls, torches in a river of green fire, and the men of Gondor giving ground across the eastern half of the broken city. By dawn the east bank is held, the bridge is down, and the thing that directs it all has already turned its attention west.

aspect.en: Smoke stands over Osgiliath permanently now; patrols of the east bank do not answer hail.

text.en: Orcs and grim men work the ruins in shifts: raising barricades in the east streets, sinking boats, watching the water. This is not a raid that will go home — it is a door being bricked open from the inside.

lore.en: A willow that has learned to sing people to sleep.

notes.en: The eldest and angriest willow in the Old Forest, rooted by the Withywindle and lord of all the rooted hatred of trees against things that go free upon the earth. He cannot walk — but the path can be persuaded to bring you to him.

aspect.en: The path through the old wood forgets the way, and the willows lean over the water closer than trees should lean.

text.en: The drowsiness is not natural — it comes in waves off the great willow like heat off a hearth, and the water at its roots sings a thin sleepy song. The crack in the trunk is exactly large enough for a careless traveller, and it has closed before.

lore.en: A wizard who would rather talk to thrushes than to wizards.

notes.en: Sent by Saruman to fetch Gandalf to Orthanc — an errand he runs in honest ignorance, as honest men are made to run bad errands. Then home to Rhosgobel, to the birds and the silence, before the world notices.

aspect.en: A queer brown-cloaked fellow rode west asking everywhere for Gandalf, as if the name were a lost dog.

text.en: A weathered man in earth-brown robes, kind-eyed and urgent, riding with a cage of small birds at his saddle. He asks every traveller the same thing: have you seen Gandalf the Grey? He does not say why he asks, and does not seem to know that the question is dangerous.

aspect.en: The brown wanderer rode back east at an easier pace, whistling to the birds, his errand done.

text.en: Radagast the Brown goes home by the easy way, stopping often to speak with jays and hedgehogs. His errand is delivered. He does not know what it will cost.

lore.en: The part of the Hunt that came inside the fence.

notes.en: Four of the Nine sent into the green country itself: Khamûl and his fellows among the hedges and lanes, sniffing out a name — Baggins of Hobbiton — house by house if they must.

aspect.en: A tall dark rider asked at a farm for Baggins — and the farmer said 'Hobbiton' and has been sorry since.

text.en: A rider, or several, in black, on the quiet lanes of the Shire at dusk. They ask politely. That is the worst of it — they ask politely for a name, Baggins, and dogs will not bark at them, and no one who answered has slept well since.

lore.en: An elf so far into his goodbye that he has passed through it and out the other side.

notes.en: He has said goodbye to everything already — house, tree, road, name — and now walks the last miles in a silence so complete that the birds keep singing around him, mistaking him for weather.

aspect.en: A grey-cloaked figure walking the shore-road alone, never at a hurry, never looking back at the hills.

text.en: He walks alone and he does not sing, and when you greet him he answers with a nod — courteous, unhurried, utterly closed. Whatever he is leaving, he has already left it. All that is left of him on the road is a direction: west.

lore.en: The Icemen name it Routa — older than their memory and exactly as patient.

notes.en: An old, slow cold-drake that has hunted the plains of Talath Uichel since before the Snowmen had words for it. It does not rage — it simply outlasts, the way winter outlasts.

aspect.en: The Icemen leave a carved bone-post at the edge of the plains and do not say why; beyond it, the wind smells of sulphur.

text.en: Beyond the carved post the plain is strangely empty — no bears, no wolves, even the cold seems to keep its distance. Then the grey ridge in the middle distance moves, and you understand the post is not a warning to the drake. It is a warning to you.

aspect.en: The Icemen say the mountain-shelter is spoken for until spring, by the smell of the forge beneath.

text.en: Under the ice the den is warm, and in the dark a slow breath keeps a rhythm that has not changed in three hundred years. The bones near the mouth are very old and very new.

lore.en: Nine black riders who were kings once. Their passing is a sickness in the land before it is ever a shape on the road.

notes.en: The Nazgûl ride again: gather the Ring. From Dol Guldur they pass the Anduin unseen, wring answers from Saruman at Isengard, and hunt a name — Baggins — across the width of Eriador.

aspect.en: Travellers south of the river speak of riders in black who passed in the night, and of a fear they could not name.

text.en: Far off, nine horsemen move across the land in a silence that is not natural. No bird crosses their path. Watching them, you feel the memory of a cold that has not reached you yet — and you understand that you must not be seen.

aspect.en: The Greenway is empty of honest travellers; at dusk a herdsman swears nine black horses drank at the ford and went on north.

text.en: They ride the old road and they are asking questions at every farm: a name, a family's name, spoken soft as a favour. The horses are blown but the riders are not tired. The riders are never tired.

aspect.en: Bree-land whispers of the raid at the inn and the shuttered doors since; out on the Road, black riders pace the wilds like a closing hand.

text.en: Five of them stand beneath the ruined tower, and the night itself seems to lean toward them. Something small and bright somewhere to the west is what they want — everything else in the world is only in the way.

aspect.en: A cold wind came out of the north that was no weather, and went south, and was gone.

text.en: The flood took their horses and their shapes, but not them. What passes south through the night now is a screaming on the wind that no throat could make — going home to their master empty-handed.

lore.en: A shepherd of trees, old as the forest, patient as the forest, dangerous as the forest.

notes.en: Fangorn, the eldest of the Ents — slow to anger, slower to decide, and lately walking his woods counting how much is still worth keeping. The hour of the Ents is coming, though he does not know it yet.

aspect.en: A sound like a very large man clearing a very deep throat, far off in the old wood — and a path of moss-deep footprints no man made.

text.en: Fourteen feet of gnarled patience stops mid-stride to look at you with eyes like wells. He is not hostile — he is deciding, and the deciding takes a little while, and everything in Fangorn waits on it.

lore.en: Two hungry idiots the size of a barn, arguing since summer.

notes.en: Two troll brothers who quarrelled their way out of a war-band over a cooking pot — Gram wants to catch sheep like a sensible troll, Podge wants 'a dwarf, proper, not this stringy rubbish', and the pot is carried by whichever one lost the last argument.

aspect.en: A clanging like a blacksmith falling downhill, and two deep voices shouting "YER TURN" at nothing the night shows.

text.en: Two hill-trolls crash through the dark carrying — between them, on a spear-haft — a cooking pot the size of a bathtub. Gram says sheep. Podge says dwarf. The argument has been running for three valleys and shows every sign of outlasting the moon. Your fire is the best thing either of them has seen all week.

lore.en: A troll-mother is a mountain with opinions — hers are called Nub and Skrit.

notes.en: Driven out of the Ettenmoors by a bigger troll's temper, Amma led her two younglings south into the Trollshaws where the picking is soft. She is teaching them to dig for roots and badgers — and still arguing with herself about whether travellers count as dinner or as trouble.

aspect.en: In the morning there are diggings like giant mole-hills, a smell of damp quarry-stone, and one deep motherly voice still arguing far off.

text.en: Three trolls in a pine-hollow at dead of night: Amma Granitecheek and her two younglings, Nub and Skrit, half her size and twice her appetite. She is teaching them to grub the ground — 'Roots, you great lumps, roots fill a belly and don't fight back' — while Skrit keeps eyeing your campfire and being swatted for it. Hungry trolls are dangerous. A troll-mother being pedagogical is something else entirely.

lore.en: A boy pretending to be a dwarf, trying to eat without being seen.

notes.en: Half-dwarf, though he would take a fist over the word 'half'. Twenty winters, a new beard tended like a garden — and hungry. He left his mother and sisters after his father's blood stayed on his hands; now he forages the Wold's edges east of Rohan, one frightened meal at a time.

aspect.en: A stocky youth foraging the field-edges — he flinches from voices like a deer but squares up like a dwarf.

text.en: A broad young figure scrabbling at a hedge-garden — unmistakably dwarf-built, unmistakably too tall. He rounds on you all bristle and knuckles until the smell of bread reaches him; fear has been driving him longer than hunger. Feed him, and he eats like a landslide and talks, carefully, of Moria and mothers.
